If we were to ask, “Which students are most likely to be addicted to their electronic gadgets?” our unit of analysis would be the individual. We might mail a survey to students on campus, and our aim would be to classify individuals according to their membership in certain social classes in order to see how membership in those classes correlated with gadget addiction. For example, we might find that majors in new media, men, and students with high socioeconomic status are all more likely than other students to become addicted to their electronic gadgets. Another possibility would be to ask, “How do students’ gadget addictions differ, and how are they similar?” In this case, we could conduct observations of addicted students and record when, where, why, and how they use their gadgets. In both cases, one using a survey and the other using observations, data are collected from individual students. In the first one, our aim is to describe the characteristics of individuals. We may then make generalizations about the populations to which these individuals belong, but our unit of analysis is still the individual. In the second study, we will observe individuals in order to describe some social phenomenon, in this case, types of gadget addictions. Groups of course vary in size, and almost no group is too small or too large to be of interest to sociologists. Families, friendship groups, and street gangs make up some of the more common microlevel groups examined by sociologists. Employees in an organization, professionals in a particular domain (e.g., chefs, lawyers, sociologists), and members of clubs (e.g., Girl Scouts, Rotary, Red Hat Society) are all mesolevel groups that sociologists might study. Finally, at the macro level, sociologists sometimes examine citizens of entire nations or residents of different continents or other regions. A study of student addictions to their electronic gadgets at the group level might consider whether certain types of social clubs have more or fewer gadget-addicted members than other sorts of clubs. Perhaps we would find that clubs that emphasize physical fitness, such as the rugby club and the scuba club, have fewer gadget-addicted members than clubs that emphasize cerebral activity, such as the chess club and the sociology club. If we had instead asked whether people who join cerebral clubs are more likely to be gadget-addicted than those who join social clubs, then our unit of analysis would have been individuals. As you may recall from your introductory sociology class, organizations include entities like corporations, colleges and universities, and even night clubs. At the organization level, a study of students’ electronic gadget addictions might ask, “How do different colleges address the problem of electronic gadget addiction?” In this case, our interest lies not in the experience of individual students but instead in the campus-to-campus differences in confronting gadget addictions. Of course, it would be silly in a textbook focused on social scientific research to neglect social phenomena as a potential unit of analysis. I mentioned one such example earlier, but let’s look more closely at this sort of unit of analysis. Many sociologists study a variety of social interactions and social problems that fall under this category. Examples include social problems like murder or rape; and other social phenomena such as voting and even gadget use or misuse. A researcher interested in students’ electronic gadget addictions could ask, “What are the various types of electronic gadget addictions that exist among students?” Perhaps the researcher will discover that some addictions are primarily centered around social media such as chat rooms, Facebook, or texting while other addictions center on gadgets such as handheld, single-player video games or DVR devices that discourage interaction with others. The resultant typology of gadget addictions would tell us something about the social phenomenon (unit of analysis) being studied. Finally, a number of social scientists examine policies and principles, the last type of unit of analysis we’ll consider here. Perhaps a researcher has been hired by a college to help it write an effective policy against electronic gadget addiction. In this case, the researcher might gather all previously written policies from campuses all over the country and compare policies at campuses where addiction rates are low to policies at campuses where addiction rates are high.

While it is true that some topics lend themselves to a particular level of inquiry, there are many topics that could be studied from any of the three levels. The choice depends on the specific interest of the researcher, the approach he or she would like to take, and the sorts of questions he or she wants to be able to answer about the topic. Gang activity has been a topic of interest to sociologists for many years and has been studied from each of the levels of inquiry described here. At the micro level, sociologists might study the inner workings of a specific gang, communication styles, and what everyday life is like for gang members. Though not written by a sociologist, one example of a microlevel analysis of gang activity can be found in Sanyika Shakur's 1993 autobiography, Monster . Shakur's recounting of experiences highlights microlevel interactions between himself, fellow Crips members, and other gangs.

candidate_draft: A paradigm is defined as an analytic lens, a way of viewing the world, and a framework from which to understand the human experience. In social science, paradigms function as a way of framing what we know, what we can know, and how we can know it. Each predominant paradigm carries its own unique ontological and epistemological perspective, and these frameworks shape our everyday view of the world. While the terms paradigm and theory are often used interchangeably, they are analytically distinct concepts; distinguishing them provides a useful framework for understanding the connections between research methods and social scientific ways of thinking. The text identifies four predominant social scientific paradigms that guide research: positivism, the critical paradigm, postmodernism, and a fourth paradigm associated with the construction of group realities. Positivism is guided by the principles of objectivity, knowability, and deductive logic, calling for a value-free sociology where researchers abandon biases to seek objective, empirical truth. The critical paradigm is focused on power, inequality, and social change. Postmodernism challenges almost every way of knowing taken for granted by social scientists, arguing that truth is never fully knowable because the researcher stamps their own truth on the investigation. The fourth paradigm is characterized by the idea that while individuals construct their own realities, groups often agree on notions of what is true, giving constructed meanings power beyond the individual creators.

candidate_system_evidence.text: For our purposes, we'll define paradigm as an analytic lens, a way of viewing the world and a framework from which to understand the human experience (Kuhn, 1962). For example, let's look at people's views on abortion. To some, abortion is a medical procedure that should be undertaken at the discretion of each individual woman who might experience an unwanted pregnancy. Chances are, if you have an opinion about this topic you are pretty certain about the veracity of your perspective. You are each operating under a set of assumptions about the way the world does-or at least should-work. Perhaps your assumptions come from your particular political perspective, which helps shape your view on a variety of social issues, or perhaps your assumptions are based on what you learned from your parents or in church. In any case, there is a paradigm that shapes your stance on the issue.

The first paradigm we'll consider, called positivism, is probably the framework that comes to mind for many of you when you think of science. Positivism is guided by the principles of objectivity, knowability, and deductive logic. Auguste Comte, whom you might recall from your introduction to sociology class as the person who coined the term sociology , argued that sociology should be a positivist science (Ritzer & Goodman, 2004). Positivism also calls for a value-free sociology, one in which researchers aim to abandon their biases and values in a quest for objective, empirical, and knowable truth.

While individuals may construct their own realities, groups-from a small one such as a married couple to large ones such as nations-often agree on notions of what is true and what 'is.' In other words, the meanings that we construct have power beyond the individual people who create them. A third paradigm is the critical paradigm. At its core, the critical paradigm is focused on power, inequality, and social change.

Finally, postmodernism is a paradigm that challenges almost every way of knowing that many social scientists take for granted (Best & Kellner, 1991). While social constructionists may argue that truth is in the eye of the beholder (or in the eye of the group that agrees on it), postmodernists may claim that we can never really know such truth because, in the studying and reporting of others' truths, the researcher stamps her or his own truth on the investigation. Finally, while the critical paradigm may argue that power, inequality, and change shape reality and truth, a postmodernist may in turn ask, whose power, whose inequality, whose change, whose reality, and whose truth? As you might imagine, the postmodernist paradigm poses quite a challenge for social scientific researchers. How does one study something that may or may not be real or that is only real in your current and unique experience of it? The terms paradigm and theory are often used interchangeably in social science, although social scientists do not always agree whether these are identical or distinct concepts. In this text, we will make a slight distinction between the two ideas because thinking about each concept as analytically distinct provides a useful framework for understanding the connections between research methods and social scientific ways of thinking.

Paradigms are a way of framing what we know, what we can know, and how we can know it. In social science, there are several predominant paradigms, each with its own unique ontological and epistemological perspective. Let's look at four of the most common social scientific paradigms that might guide you as you begin to think about conducting research.

candidate_draft: In sociological research, theory is defined as a way of explanation or an explanatory statement that fits the evidence. Theories provide a framework for looking at the world and understanding human interaction, serving to structure and inform sociological research. While paradigms may point researchers in a particular direction regarding "why" questions, theories more specifically map out the explanation, or the "how," behind those questions. Theories can vary in scope; some are sweeping in their coverage, aiming to explain the existence and continuation of society, while others are narrower in focus, aiming to understand one particular phenomenon without attempting broader explanations. The relationship between theory and research is reciprocal: theories structure and inform research, and research structures and informs theory. This relationship is evident in both inductive and deductive approaches to research, where theory is crucial but the specific relationship between theory and research differs for each approach. The theory invoked by a researcher, along with the paradigm from which they frame their work, can shape not only the questions asked but also the answers discovered. Furthermore, theories point researchers in the direction of relevant concepts and possible indicators, guiding the move from a broader level of focus to a more narrow focus. Understanding these frames and approaches is crucial for successfully embarking upon and completing research-based investigations and for responsibly reading and understanding others' work.

candidate_draft: The inductive approach is a research strategy in which a researcher begins by collecting data relevant to a topic of interest. After gathering a substantial amount of data, the researcher steps back to examine the data holistically, looking for patterns and working to develop a theory that explains those patterns. This process moves from specific observations to general propositions, effectively transitioning from data to theory. In contrast to the deductive approach, which starts with a theory and tests hypotheses, the inductive approach is driven by empirical observations. Inductive and deductive approaches can be complementary; researchers may start with a deductive framework but shift to an inductive approach when confronted with new data that requires interpretation. For example, in a study of how young men learn about menstruation, researchers analyzed written narratives to identify patterns and develop a general theory of that learning process. Similarly, in research on sexual harassment, qualitative interview data were analyzed inductively to find patterns and theorize about them, while survey data were used deductively to test hypotheses. The choice between inductive and deductive approaches determines the process by which a researcher attempts to answer their research question.

candidate_system_evidence.text: There are many good examples of inductive research, but we’ll look at just a few here. One fascinating recent study in which the researchers took an inductive approach was Katherine Allen, Christine Kaestle, and Abbie Goldberg’s study (2011) [1] of how boys and young men learn about menstruation. To understand this process, Allen and her colleagues analyzed the written narratives of 23 young men in which the men described how they learned about menstruation, what they thought of it when they first learned about it, and what they think of it now. By looking for patterns across all 23 men’s narratives, the researchers were able to develop a general theory of how boys and young men learn about this aspect of girls’ and women’s biology. They conclude that sisters play an important role in boys’ early understanding of menstruation, that menstruation makes boys feel somewhat separated from girls, and that as they enter young adulthood and form romantic relationships, young men develop more mature attitudes about menstruation.

candidate_draft: The deductive approach is a research strategy that moves from a more general level to a more specific one, typically associated with scientific investigation. It involves beginning with a theory, developing hypotheses from that theory, and then collecting and analyzing data to test those hypotheses. In this process, the researcher studies what others have done, reads existing theories of the phenomenon being studied, and then tests hypotheses that emerge from those theories. Hypotheses are typically drawn from theories and usually describe how an independent variable is expected to affect some dependent variable or variables. If the theory accurately reflects the phenomenon it is designed to explain, then the researcher’s hypotheses about what he or she will observe in the real world should bear out. The deductive approach is distinct from the inductive approach, which begins with empirical observations and moves toward theory. While inductive and deductive approaches seem quite different, they can be complementary; researchers may plan for their research to include multiple components, one inductive and the other deductive, or discover along the way that the other approach is needed to help illuminate findings. The choice between inductive and deductive approaches determines the process by which a researcher attempts to answer a research question.

candidate_system_evidence.text: Researchers taking a deductive approach take the steps described earlier for inductive research and reverse their order. That is, they move from a more general level to a more specific one. A deductive approach to research is the one that people typically associate with scientific investigation. The researcher studies what others have done, reads existing theories of whatever phenomenon he or she is studying, and then tests hypotheses that emerge from those theories.

In some cases, the purpose of research is to test a specific hypothesis or hypotheses. At other times, researchers do not have predictions about what they will find but instead conduct research to answer a question or questions, with an open-minded desire to know about a topic, or to help develop hypotheses for later testing. A hypothesis is a statement, sometimes but not always causal, describing a researcher’s expectation regarding what he or she anticipates finding. Often hypotheses are written to describe the expected relationship between two variables (though this is not a requirement). Hypotheses are typically drawn from theories and usually describe how an independent variable is expected to affect some dependent variable or variables. Researchers following a deductive approach to their research will hypothesize about what they expect to find based on the theory or theories that frame their study. If the theory accurately reflects the phenomenon it is designed to explain, then the researcher’s hypotheses about what he or she will observe in the real world should bear out.

While inductive and deductive approaches to research seem quite different, they can actually be rather complementary. In some cases, researchers will plan for their research to include multiple components, one inductive and the other deductive. In other cases, a researcher might begin a study with the plan to only conduct either inductive or deductive research, but then he or she discovers along the way that the other approach is needed to help illuminate findings. candidate_draft: Research on humans is a category of sociological inquiry distinguished by the fact that its subjects are living human beings. This characteristic is the primary factor that shapes the ethics of sociological research, as it presents a unique set of challenges and opportunities when conducting ethical research. Because of this, research on human subjects is regulated much more heavily than research on nonhuman subjects, although there are ethical considerations that all researchers must consider regardless of their research subject. Conducting research on humans presents a number of unique ethical considerations, and subjects’ identities and the information they share should be protected by researchers. How consent and identity protection are defined may vary by individual researcher, institution, or academic discipline. A norm of voluntary participation is presumed in all sociological research projects; researchers cannot force anyone to participate without that person’s knowledge or consent. Researchers must therefore design procedures to obtain subjects’ informed consent, which is defined as a subject’s voluntary agreement to participate in research based on a full understanding of the research and of the possible risks and benefits involved. In giving their informed consent, subjects may neither waive nor even appear to waive any of their legal rights. Research on human subjects has not always been regulated to the extent that it is today, and historical examples illustrate the ethical complexities involved. For instance, in a historical case, a researcher defended the ethics of his actions in the original version of his report, but in a later reprint, he added that he would conduct the second part of his research differently. Rather than trace license numbers and interview unwitting tearoom participants in their homes under the guise of public health research, he would instead spend more time in the field and work to cultivate a pool of informants who would know that he was a researcher and would be able to fully consent to being studied. This historical reflection underscores the importance of informed consent and the protection of subjects' identities and information in research on humans.

As should be clear by now, conducting research on humans presents a number of unique ethical considerations. Further, subjects’ identities and the information they share should be protected by researchers. Of course, how consent and identity protection are defined may vary by individual researcher, institution, or academic discipline. In this section, we’ll take a look at a few specific topics that individual researchers and sociologists in general must consider before embarking on research with human subjects. Informed Consent A norm of voluntary participation is presumed in all sociological research projects. In other words, we cannot force anyone to participate in our research without that person’s knowledge or consent (so much for that Truman Show experiment). Researchers must therefore design procedures to obtain subjects’ informed consent to participate in their research. Informed consent is defined as a subject’s voluntary agreement to participate in research based on a full understanding of the research and of the possible risks and benefits involved. Although it sounds simple, ensuring that one has actually obtained informed consent is a much more complex process than you might initially presume. The first requirement is that, in giving their informed consent, subjects may neither waive nor even appear to waive any of their legal rights. However, their research may involve other types of risks. For example, what if a sociological researcher fails to sufficiently conceal the identity of a subject who admits to participating in a local swinger’s club, enjoying a little sadomasochistic activity now and again or violating her marriage vows? I once advised an undergraduate student who conducted a research project on speciesism, the belief that some species are superior to or have more value and rights than others. Her research question was “Why and how do humans construct divisions between themselves and animals?” This student organized her review of literature around the two parts of her research question: In the “why” section of her literature review, she described prior research that addressed questions of why humans are sometimes speciesist. She used the same structure in the “how” section of her literature review, arranging subsections around the answers posed in previous literature about how humans construct divisions between themselves and animals. This organizational scheme helped readers understand what we already know about the topic and what theories we rely on to help make sense of the topic. Our job as researchers is to recognize and address our biases as part of the research process, if an imperfect part. We all use particular approaches, be they theories, levels of analysis, or temporal processes, to frame and conduct our work.

Specific Ethical Issues to Consider refers to the targeted ethical obligations that researchers must address when conducting studies involving human subjects. This unit distinguishes itself from general ethical frameworks by focusing on concrete procedural requirements and specific risks, such as the protection of participant identity and the prevention of harm. A foundational norm in this area is voluntary participation, which prohibits forcing anyone to participate in research without their knowledge or consent. To operationalize this norm, researchers must design procedures to obtain informed consent, defined as a subject's voluntary agreement to participate based on a full understanding of the research and its possible risks and benefits. A critical requirement of informed consent is that subjects may neither waive nor appear to waive any of their legal rights. 

The unit also addresses the distinction between anonymity and confidentiality, noting that if a researcher promises anonymity, they cannot link individual participants with their data. Furthermore, the ethical conduct of research is evaluated across micro, meso, and macro levels. At the micro level, researchers must consider their own conduct and the rights of individual participants, asking questions about whether specific actions, such as deception or the administration of perceived shocks, were ethical and whether individual rights were protected. 

These specific issues are contextualized by historical precedents, such as the Tuskegee Syphilis Experiment, where participants were denied effective treatment to observe disease progression, leading to a public apology by the U.S. government. The unit also incorporates the five general principles of the American Sociological Association’s Code of Ethics: professional competence, integrity, professional and scientific responsibility, and social responsibility. These principles require researchers to recognize their limitations, maintain honesty and fairness, and strive to advance the science of sociology while serving the public good. The interpretation of these principles and specific ethical standards can vary by individual researcher, institution, or academic discipline.

canonical_name: Ethics at Micro, Meso, and Macro Levels
candidate_draft:
Ethics at Micro, Meso, and Macro Levels is a framework for analyzing the ethical conduct of social scientific research by examining potential issues from the perspective of different analytical levels. This approach applies the micro-meso-macro framework to research ethics, providing a useful way to think about the breadth of ethical questions that might arise out of any research project.

At the micro level, researchers must consider their own conduct and the rights of individual research participants. This level of inquiry focuses on the smallest levels of interaction, such as one-on-one interactions between couples or friends, or how a person’s perception of self is influenced by their social context. Ethical considerations at this level include questions about whether a researcher behaved ethically when allowing participants to think they were administering electronic shocks to fellow participants, or when deceiving research subjects about their own identity. The core question is whether the rights of individuals in these studies were protected.

At the meso level, researchers should consider the expectations of their profession and of any organizations that may have funded their research. This level of inquiry involves investigating groups, such as how norms of workplace behavior vary across professions or how children’s sporting clubs are organized. The ethical focus here is on the broader professional and organizational context in which the research is conducted.

At the macro level, researchers should consider their duty to and the expectations of society with respect to social scientific research. This level of inquiry examines social structures and institutions, as well as large-scale patterns. For example, a study of globalization that examines the interrelationships between nations would be an example of a macrolevel study. The ethical considerations at this level are concerned with the broader societal impact and expectations of the research.

Some topics are best suited to be examined at one particular level, while other topics can be studied at each of the three different levels. This framework demonstrates that while sociologists share some common beliefs about the value of investigating and understanding human interaction, at what level they investigate that interaction will vary.

candidate_draft: The distinction between the practice of science and the uses of science separates how science is conducted from how it is understood and applied. The practice of science refers to the process and practice of research, while the uses of science encompass the ways that science is applied to create laws and social policies, to understand individuals and communities, to improve life conditions, or to support business and other undertakings. Ethical use of science requires educating oneself about the design and purpose of studies, recognizing limitations in scientific and methodological knowledge, and applying findings only to cases or populations for which they are relevant. Social scientists conducting research for organizations may face ethical questions about the use of their research, particularly when the organization controls the final report and publicity. Conflicts of interest can arise between in-house evaluation researchers and the employer being evaluated, or between independent researchers and their funding agencies. What qualifies as ethical research may shift over time and across cultures, with individual researchers and regulatory entities working to define the boundaries between ethical and unethical research.

An Institutional Review Board (IRB) is a regulatory entity tasked with ensuring that the rights and welfare of human research subjects are protected at institutions that receive federal support for research, including universities, hospitals, and nonprofit research institutions. All institutions receiving federal support for research must have an IRB, and organizations that do not receive federal support but where research is conducted also often include IRBs as part of their organizational structure. IRBs typically consist of members from a variety of disciplines, such as sociology, economics, education, social work, and communications; this diversity of membership helps ensure that the many and complex ethical issues that may arise from human subjects research are considered fully and by a knowledgeable and experienced panel.

Investigators conducting research on human subjects are required to submit proposals outlining their research plans to IRBs for review and approval prior to beginning their research. Even students who conduct research on human subjects must have their proposed work reviewed and approved by the IRB before beginning any research, though on some campuses, some exceptions are made for classroom projects that will not be shared outside of the classroom.

Most IRBs require researchers to share details about the purpose of the research, possible benefits of participation, and possible risks associated with participating in that research. In addition, researchers must describe how they will protect subjects’ identities, how and for how long any data collected will be stored, and whom to contact for additional information about the study or about subjects’ rights. All this information is typically shared in an informed consent form that researchers provide to subjects. In some cases, subjects are asked to sign the consent form indicating that they have read it and fully understand its contents. In other cases, subjects are simply provided a copy of the consent form and researchers are responsible for making sure that subjects have read and understand the form before proceeding with any kind of data collection.

IRBs also have something to say about any planned deception of research subjects. Some IRBs approve deception, but others look warily upon a field researcher engaging in covert participation. IRBs are not always popular or appreciated by researchers. In some cases, the concern is that IRBs are most well versed in reviewing biomedical and experimental research, neither of which is particularly common within sociology. Much sociological research, especially qualitative research, is open ended in nature, a fact that can be problematic for IRBs. The members of IRBs often want to know in advance exactly who will be observed, where, when, and for how long, whether and how they will be approached, exactly what questions they will be asked, and what predictions the researcher has for her or his findings. Providing this level of detail for a yearlong participant observation within an activist group of 200-plus members, for example, would be extraordinarily frustrating for the researcher in the best case and most likely would prove to be impossible. Of course, IRBs do not intend to have researchers avoid studying controversial topics or avoid using certain methodologically sound data-collection techniques, but unfortunately, that is sometimes the result. The solution is not to do away with review boards, which serve a necessary and important function, but instead to help educate IRB members about the variety of social scientific research methods and topics covered by sociologists and other social scientists.

What qualifies as ethical research may shift over time and across cultures as individual researchers; disciplinary organizations; and regulatory entities such as institutional review boards, courts, and lawmakers all work to define the boundaries between ethical and unethical research.

If you are conducting research while associated with any federally funded agency (and even many private entities), your institutional review board (IRB) probably will have something to say about any planned deception of research subjects.

It may surprise you to hear that IRBs are not always popular or appreciated by researchers. Who wouldn’t want to conduct ethical research, you ask? In some cases, the concern is that IRBs are most well versed in reviewing biomedical and experimental research, neither of which is particularly common within sociology. Much sociological research, especially qualitative research, is open ended in nature, a fact that can be problematic for IRBs. The members of IRBs often want to know in advance exactly who will be observed, where, when, and for how long, whether and how they will be approached, exactly what questions they will be asked, and what predictions the researcher has for her or his findings. Providing this level of detail for a yearlong participant observation within an activist group of 200-plus members, for example, would be extraordinarily frustrating for the researcher in the best case and most likely would prove to be impossible. Of course, IRBs do not intend to have researchers avoid studying controversial topics or avoid using certain methodologically sound data- collection techniques, but unfortunately, that is sometimes the result. The solution is not to do away with review boards, which serve a necessary and important function, but instead to help educate IRB members about the variety of social scientific research methods and topics covered by sociologists and other social scientists.

candidate_draft: Informed consent is defined as a subject's voluntary agreement to participate in research based on a full understanding of the research and of the possible risks and benefits involved. This norm of voluntary participation is presumed in all sociological research projects, meaning researchers cannot force anyone to participate without that person's knowledge or consent. Researchers must design procedures to obtain this consent, a process that is more complex than it initially appears. The first requirement is that subjects may neither waive nor even appear to waive any of their legal rights. Beyond legal issues, most institutional review boards (IRBs) require researchers to share details about the purpose of the research, possible benefits of participation, and possible risks associated with participating. Researchers must also describe how they will protect subjects' identities, how and for how long any data collected will be stored, and whom to contact for additional information about the study or subjects' rights. This information is typically shared in an informed consent form provided to subjects. In some cases, subjects are asked to sign the consent form indicating they have read and fully understand its contents; in other cases, researchers are responsible for ensuring subjects have read and understood the form before proceeding with data collection. The informed consent process includes the requirement that researchers outline how they will protect the identities of subjects, an aspect that is commonly misunderstood. In protecting subjects' identities, researchers typically promise to maintain either anonymity or confidentiality. Anonymity is the more stringent of the two, meaning not even the researcher is able to link participants' data with their identities. Anonymity may be impossible for some sociological researchers to promise because several modes of data collection, such as participant observation and face-to-face interviewing, require that researchers know the identities of their research participants. In these cases, a researcher should be able to at least promise confidentiality, which means that some identifying information on subjects is known and may be kept, but only the researcher can link participants with their data and promises not to do so publicly. Not all potential research subjects are considered equally competent or legally allowed to consent to participate in research. These subjects are sometimes referred to as members of vulnerable populations, people who may be at risk of experiencing undue influence or coercion. For example, minors must have the consent of a legal guardian in order to participate in research, and in some cases, minors themselves are also asked to participate in the consent process by signing special, age-appropriate consent forms. Prisoners and parolees also qualify as vulnerable populations, with concerns arising from the possibility that they could perceive they will receive some highly desired reward, such as early release, if they participate in research. Another potential concern is that vulnerable populations may be underrepresented in research, and even denied potential benefits of participation, specifically because of concerns about their ability to consent. Researchers must take extra care to ensure that their procedures for obtaining consent from vulnerable populations are not coercive, and the procedures for receiving approval to conduct research on these groups may be more rigorous than for nonvulnerable populations. On the other hand, researchers must work to avoid excluding members of vulnerable populations from participation simply on the grounds that they are vulnerable or that obtaining their consent may be more complex. While there is no easy solution to this double-edged sword, an awareness of the potential concerns associated with research on vulnerable populations is important for identifying whatever solution is most appropriate for a specific case. Efforts to regulate the ethical conduct of research, while necessary, are certainly not sufficient for ensuring that human subjects' rights will be honored, as illustrated by historical examples where written regulations specifying that human subjects must clearly and willingly consent to their participation in medical research were completely disregarded by experimenters.

Vulnerable populations are research subjects who are not considered equally competent or legally allowed to consent to participate in research, and who may be at risk of experiencing undue influence or coercion. This unit specifically addresses the ethical and procedural requirements for obtaining informed consent from these groups, distinguishing them from general research ethics or sampling concepts. The evidence identifies minors, prisoners, and parolees as examples of vulnerable populations. For minors, participation requires the consent of a legal guardian, and in some cases, the minors themselves sign special, age-appropriate consent forms. For prisoners and parolees, the primary concern is the potential for coercion, as these individuals might perceive that participation in research will result in highly desired rewards, such as early release. 

The ethical framework for studying vulnerable populations involves a dual obligation. On one hand, researchers must take extra care to ensure that consent procedures are not coercive, and the procedures for receiving approval to conduct research on these groups may be more rigorous than those for nonvulnerable populations. On the other hand, researchers must work to avoid excluding members of vulnerable populations from participation simply on the grounds that they are vulnerable or that obtaining their consent may be more complex. This is described as a "double-edged sword" because while protection is necessary, exclusion denies these groups the potential benefits of research participation. The goal is to identify the unique concerns related to the study of these populations to determine the most appropriate solution for a specific case.

Anonymity is the more stringent of the two protections; when a researcher promises anonymity, not even the researcher is able to link participants' data with their identities. candidate_draft: The ASA Code of Ethics is a set of ethical principles adopted by the American Sociological Association (ASA) to guide researchers in the discipline of sociology. The ASA has developed this Code of Ethics to which American sociologists are expected to adhere. The Code includes ethical guidelines for research as well as guidelines for the other roles that sociologists play, such as teaching. The Code is structured around five general principles, which are accompanied by 20 more specific ethical standards. These principles and standards must be interpreted by individual researchers, as their application can vary depending on the specific context of the research. One of the five principles is professional competence, which states that researchers should recognize their own limitations and only conduct research for which they have been properly trained. It also requires researchers to engage in ongoing education to remain competent. Another principle is social responsibility, which states that sociologists should strive to advance the science of sociology and serve the public good. The Code also addresses the principle of confidentiality, which requires that if a researcher promises anonymity, he or she cannot link individual participants with their data. The Code is a key resource for understanding the ethical obligations of sociologists in their professional roles.

The unit “Is It Sociological?” addresses the criteria for determining whether a research topic qualifies as sociological. Sociology is defined as a social science that uses organized and intentional procedures to uncover facts or truths about society, with a specific focus on patterns in society. The discipline is unique in its focus on the combination of social context, patterns, and social change. Sociologists study how individuals shape, are shaped by, and create and maintain their social groups, with the main point being that sociologists study human beings in relation to one another.

To identify a sociological research topic, it is worth considering what sociology is not. While the differences between sociology and chemical engineering may be clear, there are other disciplines with which sociology shares interests, and the lines between these disciplines may get blurred at times. Thinking about sociology’s similarities to and differences from other disciplines can help frame a research question that is indeed sociological. A research question must be empirical and sociological; for example, a question about the morality of health care approaches is not sociological, but a question about the process by which health care institutions obtain funding is empirical and sociological. The research question must be clear and focused, not just a broad topic like “child-free adults” or “movies.”

The sociological way of knowing differs from believing things because an authority says they are true. Without questioning what we think we know to be true, we may wind up believing things that are actually false. This is most likely to occur when an authority tells us that something is so. Although it is understandable that someone might believe something to be true because someone he or she looks up to or respects has said it is so, this way of knowing differs from the sociological way of knowing, which is the focus of the text. Conducting sociological research is a scholarly pursuit, and sociological researchers generally aim to reach a true understanding of social processes. It is crucial that researchers share all aspects of their research—the good, the bad, and the ugly—to ensure that others will understand, be able to build from, and effectively critique their work.

canonical_name: Qualitative or Quantitative? Some Specific Considerations
candidate_draft:
This unit addresses the specific considerations social scientists must weigh when distinguishing between qualitative and quantitative research methods. Qualitative methods are defined as ways of collecting data that yield results such as words or pictures, with common examples including field research, intensive interviews, and focus groups. In contrast, quantitative methods result in data that can be represented by and condensed into numbers; survey research is the most common quantitative method in sociology, though content analysis and interviewing can also be conducted to yield quantitative data.

A central consideration is the trade-off between depth and breadth. Qualitative methods aim to gain an in-depth understanding of a relatively small number of cases, whereas quantitative methods offer less depth but more breadth because they typically focus on a much larger number of cases. The text explicitly rejects the view that these methods are in opposition, noting that the qualitative/quantitative debate is often fueled by researchers who prefer one approach due to their specific research questions or training. Instead, the unit operates from the perspective that qualitative and quantitative methods are complementary rather than competing, as they simply have different goals, strengths, and weaknesses.

Specific considerations for qualitative interviewing include the use of semistructured, open-ended questions that allow respondents to express what they think is important in their own words. Unlike quantitative interviews, which require uniform and predetermined probing to avoid appearing to agree or disagree with respondents, qualitative interviews are designed to go with the flow of the conversation. However, qualitative interviewers should still prepare helpful probes in advance to avoid being stumped. Both approaches require the researcher to manage the power differential between themselves and respondents, take care in selecting an interview location, and recognize that the interview is a form of relationship. While field research, a qualitative method, allows for the discovery of social facts that may not be immediately obvious, it is time-intensive and emotionally taxing, sacrificing breadth for depth.

Developing good rapport requires good listening. In fact, listening during an interview is an active, not a passive, practice. Active listening means that you, the researcher, participate with the respondent by showing that you understand and follow whatever it is that he or she is telling you (Devault, 1990). Active listening probably means that you will probe the respondent for more information from time to time throughout the interview. A probe is a request for more information. Both qualitative and quantitative interviewers probe respondents, though the way they probe usually differs. In quantitative interviews, probing should be uniform. Often quantitative interviewers will predetermine what sorts of probes they will use. As an employee at the research firm I’ve mentioned before, our supervisors used to randomly listen in on quantitative telephone interviews we conducted. We were explicitly instructed not to use probes that might make us appear to agree or disagree with what respondents said. We could use “yes” or “no” if, and only if, a respondent had specifically asked us if we’d heard or understood what they had just said. In some ways qualitative interviews better lend themselves to following up with respondents and asking them to explain, describe, or otherwise provide more information. This is because qualitative interviewing techniques are designed to go with the flow and take whatever direction the respondent goes during the interview. Nevertheless, it is worth your time to come up with helpful probes in advance of an interview even in the case of a qualitative interview. You certainly do not want to find yourself stumped or speechless after a respondent has just said something about which you’d like to hear more. This is another reason that practicing your interview in advance with people who are similar to those in your sample is a good idea.

Triangulation is the practice of using multiple research strategies in a single research project. It is a methodological approach that moves beyond the either/or proposition of choosing between qualitative or quantitative data, or between idiographic or nomothetic approaches. By combining different strategies, researchers can take advantage of the strengths of various methods while simultaneously working to overcome the weaknesses of each individual method. This approach allows for a more comprehensive understanding of a topic than would be possible with a single strategy.

The evidence identifies two specific forms of triangulation. Triangulation of measures occurs when researchers use multiple approaches to measure a single variable. Triangulation of theories occurs when researchers rely on multiple theories to help explain a single event or phenomenon.

While triangulation offers analytic benefits, it is constrained by practical limitations such as limited time or funding, which may make it difficult to conduct a wide-ranging study independently. However, researchers do not necessarily have to perform all studies on their own to benefit from triangulation; they can compare their own results with existing studies or use a survey to test the generality of findings reached through field methods.

candidate_draft: Idiographic research is a research strategy in which a researcher attempts to explain or describe a phenomenon exhaustively. This approach prioritizes depth and richness of understanding over breadth, meaning that while the scope of the study may be narrower, the insight gained into the specific phenomenon or group is significantly more detailed than in broader studies. In the context of research design, choosing an idiographic approach is a decision made after determining whether the research will be exploratory, descriptive, or explanatory. It is frequently associated with qualitative methods, where the goal is to understand the multitude of specific reasons or causes that account for a behavior. For instance, a qualitative researcher studying student addiction to electronic gadgets might spend extensive time observing individuals in various settings, such as dorm rooms, classrooms, and cafeterias, to identify the specific circumstances and contexts driving their behavior. Unlike nomothetic research, which aims for general, sweeping explanations and is conducive to making statistical predictions, idiographic research is not typically used to predict when events or behaviors will occur. Instead, it focuses on understanding the 'how' of causality by examining the specific contexts in which causes and effects operate. This approach may involve intensive data collection methods, such as following a few participants for long periods or conducting lengthy, detailed interviews, and it often utilizes nonprobability sampling to seek out cases that provide deep, in-depth understanding rather than generalizable statistical trends.

A decision to conduct nomothetic research, on the other hand, means that you will aim to provide a more general, sweeping explanation or description of your topic. In this case, you sacrifice depth of understanding in favor of breadth of understanding.

What we’ve been talking about here is relationships between variables. When one variable causes another, we have what researchers call independent and dependent variables. An independent variable is one that causes another. A dependent variable is one that is caused by another. Relationship strength is another important factor to take into consideration when attempting to make causal claims if your research approach is nomothetic. I’m not talking strength of your friendships or marriage (though of course that sort of strength might affect your likelihood to keep your friends or stay married). In this context, relationship strength refers to statistical significance. The more statistically significant a relationship between two variables is shown to be, the greater confidence we can have in the strength of that relationship. For now, keep in mind that for a relationship to be considered causal, it cannot exist simply because of the chance selection of participants in a study. Qualitative research sometimes relies on quantitative work to point toward a relationship that may be interesting to investigate further. For example, if a quantitative researcher learns that men are statistically more likely than women to become addicted to their electronic gadgets, a qualitative researcher may decide to conduct some in-depth interviews and observations of men and women to learn more about how the different contexts and circumstances of men’s and women’s lives might shape their respective chances of becoming addicted. It is positioned as the counterpart to idiographic research, which attempts to explain or describe a phenomenon exhaustively. In nomothetic research, the researcher sacrifices depth of understanding in favor of breadth of understanding. This approach is often associated with quantitative studies, where researchers analyze data from larger, more representative groups to identify general factors that account for a phenomenon. For example, a nomothetic study on student addiction to electronic gadgets might use survey data to find general correlations, such as gender or behavioral tendencies, rather than exploring the specific idiosyncrasies of individual cases. When making causal claims in nomothetic research, relationship strength, defined as statistical significance, is an important factor to consider. The choice between nomothetic and idiographic approaches is a key decision in research design, made alongside decisions about whether the research is exploratory, descriptive, or explanatory.

Do you hope to gain a deep understanding of whatever phenomenon it is that you’re studying, or would you rather have a broad, but perhaps less deep, understanding? Do you want your research to be used by policymakers or others to shape social life, or is this project more about exploring your curiosities? What we’ve been talking about here is relationships between variables. When one variable causes another, we have what researchers call independent and dependent variables. An independent variable is one that causes another. A dependent variable is one that is caused by another. Relationship strength is another important factor to take into consideration when attempting to make causal claims if your research approach is nomothetic. I’m not talking strength of your friendships or marriage (though of course that sort of strength might affect your likelihood to keep your friends or stay married). In this context, relationship strength refers to statistical significance. The more statistically significant a relationship between two variables is shown to be, the greater confidence we can have in the strength of that relationship. For now, keep in mind that for a relationship to be considered causal, it cannot exist simply because of the chance selection of participants in a study. Some research methods, such as those used in qualitative and idiographic research, are not conducive to making predictions about when events or behaviors will occur. In these cases, what we are instead able to do is gain some understanding of the circumstances under which those causal relationships occur: to understand the how of causality. Qualitative research sometimes relies on quantitative work to point toward a relationship that may be interesting to investigate further. Is the research exploratory, descriptive, or explanatory? Idiographic or nomothetic? What claims does the author make about causality? Of course, it would be silly in a textbook focused on social scientific research to neglect social phenomena as a potential unit of analysis. I mentioned one such example earlier, but let’s look more closely at this sort of unit of analysis. Many sociologists study a variety of social interactions and social problems that fall under this category. Examples include social problems like murder or rape; and other social phenomena such as voting and even gadget use or misuse. A researcher interested in students’ electronic gadget addictions could ask, “What are the various types of electronic gadget addictions that exist among students?” Perhaps the researcher will discover that some addictions are primarily centered around social media such as chat rooms, Facebook, or texting while other addictions center on gadgets such as handheld, single-player video games or DVR devices that discourage interaction with others. The resultant typology of gadget addictions would tell us something about the social phenomenon (unit of analysis) being studied.

One common error we see people make when it comes to both causality and units of analysis is something called the ecological fallacy. This occurs when claims about one lower-level unit of analysis are made based on data from some higher-level unit of analysis. In many cases, this occurs when claims are made about individuals, but only group-level data have been gathered. For example, we might want to understand whether electronic gadget addictions are more common on certain campuses than on others. Perhaps different campuses around the country have provided us with their campus percentage of gadget-addicted students, and we learn from these data that electronic gadget addictions are more common on campuses that have business programs than on campuses without them. However, this would be an inappropriate conclusion to draw. Because we only have addiction rates by campus, we can only draw conclusions about campuses, not about the individual students on those campuses. The point is we simply don’t know because we only have campus-level data. By drawing conclusions about students when our data are about campuses, we run the risk of committing the ecological fallacy. On the other hand, another mistake to be aware of is reductionism. Reductionism occurs when claims about some higher-level unit of analysis are made based on data from some lower-level unit of analysis. In this case, claims about groups or macrolevel phenomena are made based on individual-level data. An example of reductionism can be seen in some descriptions of the civil rights movement. On occasion, people have proclaimed that Rosa Parks started the civil rights movement in the United States by refusing to give up her seat to a white person while on a city bus in Montgomery, Alabama, in December 1955. Although it is true that Parks played an invaluable role in the movement, and that her act of civil disobedience gave others courage to stand up against racist policies, beliefs, and actions, to credit Parks with starting the movement is reductionist. In other words, the movement is attributable to many factors—some social, others political, others economic. Of course she did—and a very important one at that. But did she cause the movement? It would be a mistake to conclude from the preceding discussion that researchers should avoid making any claims whatsoever about data or about relationships between variables. While it is important to be attentive to the possibility for error in causal reasoning about different levels of analysis, this warning should not prevent you from drawing well-reasoned analytic conclusions from your data. The point is to be cautious but not abandon entirely the social scientific quest to understand patterns of behavior. Researchers may also discuss a null hypothesis, one that predicts no relationship between the variables being studied. If a researcher rejects the null hypothesis, he or she is saying that the variables in question are somehow related to one another. Note that you will almost never hear researchers say that they have proven their hypotheses. A statement that bold implies that a relationship has been shown to exist with absolute certainty and that there is no chance that there are conditions under which the hypothesis would not bear out. Instead, researchers tend to say that their hypotheses have been supported (or not). This more cautious way of discussing findings allows for the possibility that new evidence or new ways of examining a relationship will be discovered. When testing hypotheses, social scientists generally couch their findings in terms of rejecting the null hypothesis rather than making bold statements about the relationships observed in their tables.

Triangulation is a research design approach that involves using a combination of multiple and different research strategies within a single research project. Rather than treating research design as an either/or proposition—such as choosing exclusively between qualitative and quantitative data collection, or between idiographic and nomothetic approaches—triangulation allows researchers to combine approaches to gain a more complete understanding of a topic. The primary benefit of triangulation is that it allows researchers to take advantage of the strengths of various methods while simultaneously working to overcome some of each method's weaknesses. 

The evidence identifies two specific forms of triangulation. Triangulation of measures occurs when researchers use multiple approaches to measure a single variable. Triangulation of theories occurs when researchers rely on multiple theories to help explain a single event or phenomenon. 

Practically, triangulation can be implemented by combining different data collection methods, such as conducting a survey, performing a content analysis of policies, and making observations in natural environments. Researchers do not necessarily have to conduct all components of a triangulated study on their own; they can compare their own results (such as one-on-one interviews) with findings from other methods (such as surveys or field methods) to test the generality of their findings. A key limitation of triangulation is that it may require more resources, as researchers may face limited time or funding to conduct such wide-ranging studies.

In social science, measurement is a process that occurs at multiple stages of conducting research, beginning once a research question has been identified and the researcher starts to think about the key ideas they hope to learn from the project. The measurement process involves multiple steps, including identifying key terms, defining them, figuring out how to observe them, and determining how to know if the observations are any good. An additional step involves deciding what elements a measure contains; these elements might be straightforward and directly observable, or they might be more complex and require the researcher to account for different themes or types. Social scientists measure a wide variety of things, including observational terms, indirect observables, and constructs. Because measurement is a complex process, some concepts are more complex to measure than others; for example, measuring a person's political party affiliation is less complex than measuring their sense of alienation. Measurement is critical to successful social scientific research, much as it is to successful baking, and respecting its value is of great benefit to researchers.

At the nominal level of measurement, variable attributes meet the criteria of exhaustiveness and mutual exclusivity. This is the most basic level of measurement. Relationship status, gender, race, political party affiliation, and religious affiliation are all examples of nominal-level variables. For example, to measure relationship status, we might ask respondents to tell us if they are currently partnered or single. These two attributes pretty much exhaust the possibilities for relationship status (i.e., everyone is always one or the other of these), and it is not possible for a person to simultaneous occupy more than one of these statuses (e.g., if you are single, you cannot also be partnered). Thus this measure of relationship status meets the criteria that nominallevel attributes must be exhaustive and mutually exclusive. One unique feature of nominal-level measures is that they cannot be mathematically quantified. We cannot say, for example, that being partnered has more or less quantifiable value than being single (note we're not talking here about the economic impact of one's relationship status-we're talking only about relationship status on its own, not in relation to other variables).

candidate_draft: Conceptualization is a process that involves coming up with clear, concise definitions for key concepts. It is part of the measurement process and is distinct from operationalization, which focuses on knowing how to observe concepts when collecting data. The process begins with brainstorming about the images or notions conjured up by a term and playing around with possible definitions. Researchers should then consult prior research and theory to understand how other scholars have defined the concepts, which helps compare new conceptualizations with predominant ones and decide whether to challenge or rely on existing definitions. A conceptualization is not complete until every term used within the definition is clear and makes sense to others. Some concepts have multiple elements or dimensions, meaning there are multiple components that make up a single concept; researchers must consider whether these dimensions are relevant to their specific research goals. A key caution associated with conceptualization is avoiding reification, which is the error of assuming that abstract concepts exist in a concrete, tangible way beyond the definitions assigned to them. Terms mean only what the researcher says they mean, and definitions are social agreements rather than inherent realities.

So far the word concept has come up quite a bit, and it would behoove us to make sure we have a shared understanding of that term. A concept is the notion or image that we conjure up when we think of some cluster of related observations or ideas. For example, masculinity is a concept. What do you think of when you hear that word? Presumably you imagine some set of behaviors and perhaps even a particular style of self presentation. Of course, we can't necessarily assume that everyone conjures up the same set of ideas or images when they hear the word masculinity . In fact, there are many possible ways to define the term. And while some definitions may be more common or have more support than others, there isn't one true, always-correct-in-all-settings definition. What counts as masculine may shift over time, from culture to culture, and even from individual to individual (Kimmel, 2008).

So how do we define our concepts? This is part of the process of measurement, and this portion of the process is called conceptualization. Conceptualization involves writing out clear, concise definitions for our key concepts. Sticking with the previously mentioned example of masculinity, think about what comes to mind when you read that term. How do you know masculinity when you see it? Does it have something to do with men? If so, perhaps we could define masculinity as the social norms that men are expected to follow. That seems like a reasonable start, and at this early stage of conceptualization, brainstorming about the images conjured up by concepts and playing around with possible definitions is appropriate. But this is just the first step. It would make sense as well to consult other previous research and theory to understand if other scholars have already defined the concepts we're interested in. This doesn't necessarily mean we must use their definitions, but understanding how concepts have been defined in the past will give us an idea about how our conceptualizations compare with the predominant ones out there. Understanding prior definitions of our key concepts will also help us decide whether we plan to challenge those conceptualizations or rely on them for our own work.

At the same time that you work to identify a clear research question, you will probably also think about the overarching goals of your research project. Will your approach be idiographic or nomothetic, inductive or deductive? How you design your project might also be determined in part by whether you aim for your research to have some direct application or if your goal is to contribute more generally to sociological knowledge about your topic. These will help you identify the key concepts you will study. Once you have identified those concepts, you’ll need to decide how to define them, and how you’ll know that you’re observing them when it comes time to collect your data. Defining your concepts, and knowing them when you see them, has to do with conceptualization and operationalization, the focus of . Of course, you also need to know what approach you will take to collect your data. Thus identifying your research method is another important part of research design. You also need to think about who your research participants will be and what larger group(s) they may represent. Last, but certainly not least, you should consider any potential ethical concerns that could arise during the course of your research project. These concerns might come up during your data collection, but they might also arise when you get to the point of analyzing or sharing your research results.

candidate_draft: Operationalization is the process by which a researcher spells out precisely how a concept will be measured. It involves identifying the specific research procedures used to gather data about the concepts under study. This process requires that the researcher know what research methods will be employed to learn about the concepts. Operationalization works by identifying specific indicators that will be taken to represent the ideas being studied. For example, if a researcher is interested in studying masculinity, indicators for that concept might include social roles prescribed to men in society, such as breadwinning or fatherhood. Being a breadwinner or a father might therefore be considered indicators of a person's masculinity, and the extent to which a man fulfills these roles might be understood as clues about the extent to which he is viewed as masculine. Another example involves Gallup researchers who poll 1,000 randomly selected Americans daily about their well-being. They use six factors—physical health, emotional health, work environment, life evaluation, healthy behaviors, and access to basic necessities—as indicators of the concept of well-being. Identifying indicators can also be simpler; for the concept of gender, reasonable indicators might include "woman" and "man," and potentially "other." For political party in the United States, likely indicators include Democrat and Republican. The measurement process generally involves going from a more general focus to a narrower one, but the process does not proceed in exactly the same way for all research projects. Operationalization is distinct from conceptualization, which involves defining the terms, and from reliability and validity, which are aspects of measurement quality that ensure the measures are consistent and meaningful.

But measurement is sometimes a complex process, and some concepts are more complex than others. Measuring a person’s political party affiliation, for example, is less complex than measuring her or his sense of alienation. First, we’ll take a look at the various levels of measurement that exist, and then we’ll consider a couple strategies for capturing the complexities of the concepts we wish to measure. Levels of Measurement When social scientists measure concepts, they sometimes use the language of variables and attributes. A variable refers to a grouping of several characteristics. Attributes are those characteristics. A variable’s attributes determine its level of measurement. There are four possible levels of measurement; they are nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio. At the nominal level of measurement, variable attributes meet the criteria of exhaustiveness and mutual exclusivity. This is the most basic level of measurement. Relationship status, gender, race, political party affiliation, and religious affiliation are all examples of nominal-level variables. For example, to measure relationship status, we might ask respondents to tell us if they are currently partnered or single. These two attributes pretty much exhaust the possibilities for relationship status (i.e., everyone is always one or the other of these), and it is not possible for a person to simultaneous occupy more than one of these statuses (e.g., if you are single, you cannot also be partnered). Thus this measure of relationship status meets the criteria that nominal- level attributes must be exhaustive and mutually exclusive. One unique feature of nominal-level measures is that they cannot be mathematically quantified. We cannot say, for example, that being partnered has more or less quantifiable value than being single (note we’re not talking here about the economic impact of one’s relationship status—we’re talking only about relationship status on its own, not in relation to other variables). Unlike nominal-level measures, attributes at the ordinal level can be rank ordered, though we cannot calculate a mathematical distance between those attributes. We can simply say that one attribute of an ordinal-level variable is more or less than another attribute. Ordinal-level attributes are also exhaustive and mutually exclusive, as with nominal-level variables. Examples of ordinal-level measures include social class, degree of support for policy initiatives, television program rankings, and prejudice. Thus while we can say that one person’s support for some public policy may be more or less than his neighbor’s level of support, we cannot say exactly how much more or less.

candidate_draft: A concept is the notion or image that a person conjures up when thinking of a cluster of related observations or ideas. Because different individuals may associate different sets of ideas or images with the same term, there is no single, universally correct definition for a concept in all settings; instead, multiple definitions may exist, with some being more common or supported than others. In the context of research, a concept serves as a key term that must be clearly defined before it can be measured. This definition process, known as conceptualization, involves writing out clear and concise definitions for these key concepts. Conceptualization is not merely a random brainstorming exercise; it requires ensuring that all terms used within the definition are themselves defined, and it often involves consulting prior scholarly research to understand how the concept has been defined by other scholars. This consultation helps researchers decide whether to challenge existing conceptualizations or rely on them. A critical caution in this process is avoiding reification, which is the erroneous assumption that an abstract concept exists as a concrete, tangible entity simply because a definition for it exists. Concepts are distinct from the operationalization process, which is the subsequent step of spelling out precisely how the concept will be measured through specific research procedures.

So how do we define our concepts? This is part of the process of measurement, and this portion of the process is called conceptualization. Conceptualization involves writing out clear, concise definitions for our key concepts. Sticking with the previously mentioned example of masculinity, think about what comes to mind when you read that term. How do you know masculinity when you see it? Does it have something to do with men? If so, perhaps we could define masculinity as the social norms that men are expected to follow. That seems like a reasonable start, and at this early stage of conceptualization, brainstorming about the images conjured up by concepts and playing around with possible definitions is appropriate. This doesn’t necessarily mean we must use their definitions, but understanding how concepts have been defined in the past will give us an idea about how our conceptualizations compare with the predominant ones out there. Understanding prior definitions of our key concepts will also help us decide whether we plan to challenge those conceptualizations or rely on them for our own work.

But this is just the first step. It would make sense as well to consult other previous research and theory to understand if other scholars have already defined the concepts we're interested in. This doesn't necessarily mean we must use their definitions, but understanding how concepts have been defined in the past will give us an idea about how our conceptualizations compare with the predominant ones out there. Understanding prior definitions of our key concepts will also help us decide whether we plan to challenge those conceptualizations or rely on them for our own work.

If you’ve ever met more than one man in your life, you’ve probably noticed that they are not all exactly the same, even if they live in the same society and at the same historical time period. This could mean that there are dimensions of masculinity. In terms of social scientific measurement, concepts can be said to have dimensions when there are multiple elements that make up a single concept. With respect to the term masculinity, dimensions could be regional (Is masculinity defined differently in different regions of the same country?), age based (Is masculinity defined differently for men of different ages?), or perhaps power based (Are some forms of masculinity valued more than others?). In any of these cases, the concept masculinity would be considered to have multiple dimensions. While it isn’t necessarily a must to spell out every possible dimension of the concepts you wish to measure, it may be important to do so depending on the goals of your research. The point here is to be aware that some concepts have dimensions and to think about whether and when dimensions may be relevant to the concepts you intend to investigate.
