This idea, assuming that our abstract concepts exist in some concrete, tangible way, is known as reification. To better understand reification, take a moment to think about the concept of social structure. This concept is central to sociological thinking. When we sociologists talk about social structure, we are talking about an abstract concept. Social structures shape our ways of being in the world and of interacting with one another, but they do not exist in any concrete or tangible way. A social structure isn’t the same thing as other sorts of structures, such as buildings or bridges. Sure, both types of structures are important to how we live our everyday lives, but one we can touch, and the other is just an idea that shapes our way of living. Here’s another way of thinking about reification: Think about the term family. If you were interested in studying this concept, we’ve learned that it would be good to consult prior theory and research to understand how the term has been conceptualized by others. Think, for example, about where we’d be today if we used the same definition of family that was used, say, 100 years ago. How have our understandings of this concept changed over time? What role does conceptualization in social scientific research play in our cultural understandings of terms like family? The point is that our terms mean nothing more and nothing less than whatever definition we assign to them. Sure, it makes sense to come to some social agreement about what various concepts mean. Without that agreement, it would be difficult to navigate through everyday living. But at the same time, we should not forget that we have assigned those definitions and that they are no more real than any other, alternative definition we might choose to assign.

You might be asking yourself why you should bother defining a term for which there is no single, correct definition. Believe it or not, this is true for any concept you might measure in a sociological study-there is never a single, always-correct definition. When we conduct empirical research, our terms mean only what we say they mean-nothing more and nothing less. There's a New Yorker cartoon that aptly represents this idea (http://www.cartoonbank.com/1998/it-all-depends-on-how-you-define-chop/invt/117721). Young George is looking up at a frowning adult who is standing over him, arms crossed. Without a shared understanding of this term, our understandings of what George has just done may differ. Likewise, without understanding how a researcher has defined her or his key concepts, it would be nearly impossible to understand the meaning of that researcher's findings and conclusions. Thus any decision we make based on findings from empirical research should be made based on full knowledge not only of how the research was designed, as described in Chapter 5 "Research Design", but also of how its concepts were defined and measured.

It also implies that roles, behaviors, and meanings may vary across societies and over time. candidate_draft: Operationalization is the process by which a researcher spells out precisely how a concept will be measured. It involves identifying the specific research procedures used to gather data about the concepts under study, which requires knowing the research methods to be employed. Operationalization works by identifying specific indicators that are taken to represent the ideas being studied. For example, if studying masculinity, indicators might include social roles prescribed to men, such as breadwinning or fatherhood; the extent to which a person fulfills these roles serves as clues about the extent to which they are viewed as masculine. Similarly, Gallup researchers use factors like physical health, emotional health, and work environment as indicators of the concept of well-being. Moving from identifying concepts to conceptualizing them and then to operationalizing them is a matter of increasing specificity. The researcher begins with a general interest, identifies essential concepts, defines them, and then spells out precisely how to measure them, resulting in a narrower focus. While the measurement process generally involves moving from a general focus to a narrower one, it does not proceed in exactly the same way for all research projects.

candidate_draft: An indicator is a specific measure or clue used to represent an abstract concept during the operationalization of research. Operationalization is the process of spelling out precisely how a concept will be measured by identifying the specific research procedures and data collection strategies to be employed. Indicators serve as the concrete elements that researchers use to gather data about the ideas they are studying. For example, social roles such as breadwinning or fatherhood can function as indicators of the concept of masculinity, where the extent to which these roles are fulfilled provides clues about how a person is viewed in relation to that concept. Similarly, in the context of gender, categories such as 'woman' and 'man' serve as reasonable indicators, while in the United States, political affiliations like Democrat and Republican are indicators of political party. Indicators can also be combined into more complex measures; for instance, an index is a type of measure that contains several indicators to summarize a more general concept, such as using multiple factors to measure well-being. The selection of indicators should not be arbitrary; researchers are advised to consult prior theoretical and empirical work to identify relevant concepts and to consider how their specific data-collection strategy, such as a survey or field research, will shape the operationalization of their key concepts.

Earlier I mentioned that some concepts have dimensions. To account for a concept's dimensions a researcher might rely on indexes, scales, or typologies. An index is a type of measure that contains several indicators and is used to summarize some more general concept. Rather than ask respondents how well they think they are, Gallup has designed an index that includes multiple indicators of the more general concept of well-being (http://www.gallup.com/poll/123215/Gallup-Healthways-Index.aspx).

Sexual harassment is a concept for which there are also indexes. A sexual harassment index would use multiple items to measure the singular concept of sexual harassment. For example, you might ask research participants if they have ever experienced any of the following in the workplace: offensive sexual joking, exposure to offensive materials, unwanted touching, sexual threats, or sexual assault. These five indicators all have something to do with workplace sexual harassment. On their own, some of the more benign indicators, such as joking, might not be considered harassment (unless severe or pervasive), but collectively, the experience of these behaviors might add up to an overall experience of sexual harassment. The index allows the researcher in this case to better understand what shape a respondent’s harassment experience takes. If the researcher had only asked whether a respondent had ever experienced sexual harassment at work, she wouldn’t know what sorts of behaviors actually made up that respondent’s experience. Further, if the researcher decides to rank order the various behaviors that make up sexual harassment, perhaps weighting sexual assault more heavily than joking, then she will have created a scale rather than an index.

One way to avoid taking an overly casual approach in identifying indicators, as described previously, is to turn to prior theoretical and empirical work in your area. Theories will point you in the direction of relevant concepts and possible indicators; empirical work will give you some very specific examples of how the important concepts in an area have been measured in the past and what sorts of indicators have been used. Perhaps it makes sense to use the same indicators as researchers who have come before you. candidate_draft: Reliability in measurement is a matter of consistency. A measure is considered reliable if, when the same measure is applied consistently to the same person, the result will be the same each time. This concept is distinct from validity, which is a matter of social agreement or shared understanding; while reliability focuses on the consistency of the measurement process, validity concerns whether the measure accurately captures the intended meaning of the concept. Reliability can be an issue even when researchers are not reliant on others to accurately report their behaviors. For example, a field researcher observing alcohol intake in a public location may face reliability problems if she is unable to observe every instance of patrons consuming drinks, such as when she is briefly away. In social scientific measures, memory is a common problem of reliability; if research participants are asked to recall past behaviors, the recollection process should be made as simple and straightforward as possible to ensure consistent responses. When social scientists measure concepts, they aim to achieve both reliability and validity in their measures to ensure that their findings have meaning and that the measures are of high quality.

candidate_system_evidence.text: While reliability is about consistency, validity is about shared understanding. If not, then we may be facing a problem of validity.

Reliability can be an issue even when we’re not reliant on others to accurately report their behaviors. Perhaps a field researcher is interested in observing how alcohol intake influences interactions in public locations. She may decide to conduct observations at a local pub, noting how many drinks patrons consume and how their behavior changes as their intake changes. But what if the researcher has to use the restroom and misses the three shots of tequila that the person next to her downs during the brief period she is away? The reliability of this researcher’s measure of alcohol intake, counting numbers of drinks she observes patrons consume, depends on her ability to actually observe every instance of patrons consuming drinks. If she is unlikely to be able to observe every such instance, then perhaps her mechanism for measuring this concept is not reliable.
• Reliability is a matter of consistency.
• Validity is a matter of social agreement.

Unless a person keeps a journal documenting their intake, there will very likely be some inaccuracies in their responses. If, on the other hand, we ask a person how many drinks of any kind he or she has consumed in the past week, we might get a more accurate set of responses. Validity While reliability is about consistency, validity is about shared understanding. What image comes to mind for you when you hear the word alcoholic? Are you certain that the image you conjure up is similar to the image others have in mind? If not, then we may be facing a problem of validity. To be valid, we must be certain that our measures accurately get at the meaning of our concepts. Think back to the first possible measure of alcoholism we considered in the subsection “Reliability.” There, we initially considered measuring alcoholism by asking research participants the following question: Have you ever had a problem with alcohol? We realized that this might not be the most reliable way of measuring alcoholism because the same person’s response might vary dramatically depending on how he or she is feeling that day. Likewise, this measure of alcoholism is not particularly valid. What is “a problem” with alcohol? For some, it might be having had a single regrettable or embarrassing moment that resulted from consuming too much. For others, the threshold for “problem” might be different; perhaps a person has had numerous embarrassing drunken moments but still gets out of bed for work every day so doesn’t perceive himself or herself to have a problem. Because what each respondent considers to be problematic could vary so dramatically, our measure of alcoholism isn’t likely to yield any useful or meaningful results if our aim is to objectively understand, say, how many of our research participants are alcoholics. Perhaps we’re interested in learning about a person’s dedication to healthy living. Most of us would probably agree that engaging in regular exercise is a sign of healthy living, so we could measure healthy living by counting the number of times per week that a person visits his local gym. At first this might seem like a reasonable measure, but if this respondent’s gym is anything like some of the gyms I’ve seen, there exists the distinct possibility that his gym visits include activities that are decidedly not fitness related. Perhaps he visits the gym to use their tanning beds, not a particularly good indicator of healthy living, or to flirt with potential dates or sit in the sauna. These activities, while potentially relaxing, are probably not the best indicators of healthy living. Therefore, recording the number of times a person visits the gym may not be the most valid way to measure his or her dedication to healthy living. So we wouldn’t really be measuring what we intended to measure.
• Reliability is a matter of consistency. • Validity is a matter of social agreement.

If we measure alcoholism in this way, it seems likely that anyone who identifies as an alcoholic would respond with a yes to the question. So this must be a good way to identify our group of interest, right? Would responses differ after a wild night out from what they would have been the day before? Might a teetotaler's current headache from the single glass of wine he had last night influence how he answers the question this morning? candidate_draft: Validity is a property of measurement defined by social agreement and shared understanding. It is distinct from reliability, which is a matter of consistency; while reliability concerns whether a measure yields the same result when applied consistently, validity concerns whether the measure accurately captures the intended meaning of the concept. To be valid, a measure must be certain to accurately get at the meaning of the concept it is designed to assess. No measure is exact, but some are more accurate than others, much like a portrait that approximates the look of the person it represents rather than a caricature. A common way to ensure validity is to discuss measures with others to verify that the intended meaning is shared. Validity can be compromised when the operational definition of a concept is ambiguous or when the measurement instrument fails to capture the specific phenomenon of interest. For example, measuring alcoholism by asking if a person has had a "problem" with alcohol is not valid because the threshold for what constitutes a problem varies dramatically between individuals. Similarly, measuring dedication to healthy living by counting gym visits is not valid because gym visits may include activities unrelated to fitness, such as using tanning beds or saunas. Validity can also be a problem in survey research, where the need to ask general questions that a broad range of people can understand may limit the ability to comprehensively examine a topic, potentially making survey results less valid than those obtained through methods that allow for more in-depth examination.

candidate_system_evidence.text: Reliability can be an issue even when we're not reliant on others to accurately report their behaviors. Perhaps a field researcher is interested in observing how alcohol intake influences interactions in public locations. She may decide to conduct observations at a local pub, noting how many drinks patrons consume and how their behavior changes as their intake changes. But what if the researcher has to use the restroom and misses the three shots of tequila that the person next to her downs during the brief period she is away? The reliability of this researcher's measure of alcohol intake, counting numbers of drinks she observes patrons consume, depends on her ability to actually observe every instance of patrons consuming drinks. If she is unlikely to be able to observe every such instance, then perhaps her mechanism for measuring this concept is not reliable.

While reliability is about consistency, validity is about shared understanding. What image comes to mind for you when you hear the word alcoholic ? Are you certain that the image you conjure up is similar to the image others have in mind? If not, then we may be facing a problem of validity.

Let's consider another example. Perhaps we're interested in learning about a person's dedication to healthy living. Most of us would probably agree that engaging in regular exercise is a sign of healthy living, so we could measure healthy living by counting the number of times per week that a person visits his local gym. At first this might seem like a reasonable measure, but if this respondent's gym is anything like some of the gyms I've seen, there exists the distinct possibility that his gym visits include activities that are decidedly not fitness related. Perhaps he visits the gym to use their tanning beds, not a particularly good indicator of healthy living, or to flirt with potential dates or sit in the sauna. These activities, while potentially relaxing, are probably not the best indicators of healthy living. Therefore, recording the number of times a person visits the gym may not be the most valid way to measure his or her dedication to healthy living. Using this measure wouldn't really give us an indication of a person's dedication to healthy living. So we wouldn't really be measuring what we intended to measure.

One way to think of validity is to think of it as you would a portrait. Some portraits of people look just like the actual person they are intended to represent. But other representations of people's images, such as caricatures and stick drawings, are not nearly as accurate. While a portrait may not be an exact representation of how a person looks, what's important is the extent to which it approximates the look of the person it is intended to represent. The same goes for validity in measures. No measure is exact, but some measures are more accurate than others.

canonical_name: Levels of Measurement (Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio)
candidate_draft: In social science, variables are classified into four levels of measurement: nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio. A variable is a grouping of several characteristics, and its attributes determine its level of measurement. The nominal level is the most basic; its attributes must be exhaustive and mutually exclusive, and they cannot be mathematically quantified. Examples include relationship status, gender, race, political party affiliation, and religious affiliation. The ordinal level allows attributes to be rank-ordered, but the mathematical distance between them cannot be calculated. Ordinal attributes are also exhaustive and mutually exclusive. Examples include social class, degree of support for policy initiatives, television program rankings, and prejudice. The interval level meets the criteria of the preceding levels and adds that the distance between attributes is known to be equal. This allows researchers to say how much more or less one attribute differs from another, but not the ratio of one attribute to another. Examples include IQ scores and temperatures. The ratio level is the most comprehensive; attributes are mutually exclusive, exhaustive, rank-ordered, have equal distances, and possess a true zero point. This allows for the calculation of ratios between attributes. Examples include age and years of education. The level of measurement determines the appropriate measure of central tendency: the mode for nominal variables, the median for ordinal variables, and the mean for interval and ratio variables.

candidate_system_evidence.text: When social scientists measure concepts, they sometimes use the language of variables and attributes. A variable refers to a grouping of several characteristics. Attributes are those characteristics. A variable's attributes determine its level of measurement. There are four possible levels of measurement; they are nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio.

At the nominal level of measurement, variable attributes meet the criteria of exhaustiveness and mutual exclusivity. This is the most basic level of measurement. Relationship status, gender, race, political party affiliation, and religious affiliation are all examples of nominal-level variables. For example, to measure relationship status, we might ask respondents to tell us if they are currently partnered or single. These two attributes pretty much exhaust the possibilities for relationship status (i.e., everyone is always one or the other of these), and it is not possible for a person to simultaneous occupy more than one of these statuses (e.g., if you are single, you cannot also be partnered). Thus this measure of relationship status meets the criteria that nominallevel attributes must be exhaustive and mutually exclusive. One unique feature of nominal-level measures is that they cannot be mathematically quantified. We cannot say, for example, that being partnered has more or less quantifiable value than being single (note we're not talking here about the economic impact of one's relationship status-we're talking only about relationship status on its own, not in relation to other variables).

These two attributes pretty much exhaust the possibilities for relationship status (i.e., everyone is always one or the other of these), and it is not possible for a person to simultaneous occupy more than one of these statuses (e.g., if you are single, you cannot also be partnered). Thus this measure of relationship status meets the criteria that nominal- level attributes must be exhaustive and mutually exclusive. One unique feature of nominal-level measures is that they cannot be mathematically quantified. We cannot say, for example, that being partnered has more or less quantifiable value than being single (note we’re not talking here about the economic impact of one’s relationship status—we’re talking only about relationship status on its own, not in relation to other variables). Unlike nominal-level measures, attributes at the ordinal level can be rank ordered, though we cannot calculate a mathematical distance between those attributes. We can simply say that one attribute of an ordinal-level variable is more or less than another attribute. Ordinal-level attributes are also exhaustive and mutually exclusive, as with nominal-level variables. Examples of ordinal-level measures include social class, degree of support for policy initiatives, television program rankings, and prejudice. Thus while we can say that one person’s support for some public policy may be more or less than his neighbor’s level of support, we cannot say exactly how much more or less.

Another form of univariate analysis that survey researchers can conduct on single variables is measures of central tendency. Measures of central tendency can be taken for any level variable of those we learned about in Chapter 6 "Defining and Measuring Concepts", from nominal to ratio. There are three kinds of measures of central tendency: modes, medians, and means. Modes are most appropriate for nominal-level variables. A median is the middle point in a distribution of responses. Median is the appropriate measure of central tendency for ordinal-level variables. Finally, the measure of central tendency used for interval- and ratio-level variables is the mean. To obtain a mean, one must add the value of all responses on a given variable and then divide that number of the total number of responses.

At the interval level, measures meet all the criteria of the two preceding levels, plus the distance between attributes is known to be equal. IQ scores are interval level, as are temperatures. Interval-level variables are not particularly common in social science research, but their defining characteristic is that we can say how much more or less one attribute differs from another. We cannot, however, say with certainty what the ratio of one attribute is in comparison to another. For example, it would not make sense to say that 50 degrees is half as hot as 100 degrees.

Unlike nominal-level measures, attributes at the ordinal level can be rank ordered, though we cannot calculate a mathematical distance between those attributes. We can simply say that one attribute of an ordinal-level variable is more or less than another attribute. Ordinal-level attributes are also exhaustive and mutually exclusive, as with nominal-level variables. Examples of ordinal-level measures include social class, degree of support for policy initiatives, television program rankings, and prejudice. Thus while we can say that one person’s support for some public policy may be more or less than his neighbor’s level of support, we cannot say exactly how much more or less.

Finally, at the ratio level, attributes are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, attributes can be rank ordered, the distance between attributes is equal, and attributes have a true zero point. Thus with these variables, we can say what the ratio of one attribute is in comparison to another. Examples of ratio-level variables include age and years of education. We know, for example, that a person who is 12 years old is twice as old as someone who is 6 years old.

candidate_draft: A typology is a methodological tool used to categorize concepts according to particular themes. It functions by classifying a broad concept into distinct types, which helps make the concept more meaningful and simplifies its complexities. For example, a typology of suicide identified four types: altruistic, egoistic, anomic, and fatalistic. Similarly, a typology of sexual harassment distinguishes between quid pro quo and hostile work environment forms. In both cases, the typology allows researchers to better understand the forms a concept can take and to identify what is being observed and measured. Typologies are used to condense large amounts of information and to make sense of the concepts under study.

candidate_system_evidence.text: A typology, on the other hand, is a way of categorizing concepts according to particular themes. For example, in his classic study of suicide, Emile Durkheim (1897) [1] identified four types of suicide including altruistic, egoistic, anomic, and fatalistic. Each of these types is linked to the concept of suicide, but the typology allows us to classify suicide in ways that make the concept more meaningful and that help simplify the complexities of the concept.

Sexual harassment is a concept for which there exist indexes, scales, and typologies. One typology of harassment, used in the US legal system, includes two forms of harassment: quid pro quo and hostile work environment (Blackstone & McLaughlin, 2009). Hostile work environment harassment, on the other hand, refers to sexual conduct or materials in the workplace that unreasonably interfere with a person’s ability to perform her or his job. While both types are sexual harassment, the typology helps us better understand the forms that sexual harassment can take and, in turn, helps us as researchers better identify what it is that we are observing and measuring when we study workplace harassment.

In sum, indexes and typologies are tools that researchers use to condense large amounts of information, to simplify complex concepts, and most generally, to make sense of the concepts that they study.

candidate_draft: In social scientific research, a population is defined as the cluster of people, events, things, or other phenomena that a researcher is most interested in; it represents the 'who' or 'what' the researcher aims to describe or analyze at the conclusion of a study. While populations can be broad, such as 'the American people,' they are typically specified with more precision, such as adults over a certain age or specific legal residents. A sample, in contrast, is the specific cluster of people or events from or about which the researcher actually gathers data. Sampling involves the selection of the observations that will be analyzed. Although a population and a sample might be one and the same, they are more often distinct, as it is rare for a researcher to gather data from their entire population of interest due to constraints in time and resources. Some sampling strategies allow researchers to make claims about populations much larger than their actual sample with a fair amount of confidence, while others are designed to make theoretical contributions rather than sweeping claims about large populations. Researchers must make choices about sampling and remain honest about the limitations of their study based on the sample from whom data was actually collected.

For example, a large study for which the population of interest really is the American people will likely specify which American people, such as adults over the age of 18 or citizens or legal residents. A sample, on the other hand, is the cluster of people or events, for example, from or about which you will actually gather data. Some sampling strategies allow researchers to make claims about populations that are much larger than their actually sample with a fair amount of confidence. Other sampling strategies are designed to allow researchers to make theoretical contributions rather than to make sweeping claims about large populations.

What they fail to realize, however, is that they are not alone. One of the most surprising and frustrating lessons research methods students learn is that there is a difference between one’s population of interest and one’s study sample. While there are certainly exceptions, more often than not a researcher’s population and her or his sample are not the same.

Probability sampling refers to sampling techniques in which the likelihood of a person or event being selected for membership in the sample is known. This distinguishes it from nonprobability sampling, where such likelihoods are not known. The primary goal of probability sampling is to obtain a representative sample, which resembles the population in all ways important to the research, thereby enabling generalizability. Generalizability is the key feature that distinguishes probability samples from nonprobability samples, as it allows study results to inform conclusions about a group larger than the sample itself. A core principle of probability sampling is random selection, which ensures that all elements in the target population have an equal chance of being selected. This principle allows researchers to estimate sampling error, defined as the statistical difference between sample results and the actual parameters of the population.

There are four main types of probability samples: simple random, systematic, stratified, and cluster. Simple random sampling is the most basic type, involving the creation of a sampling frame (a list of every population element), sequential numbering, and random selection using a random number table or generator. Systematic sampling is less tedious and involves selecting every kth element from the list, where k is the selection interval calculated by dividing the total population size by the desired sample size. Stratified sampling is used when a subgroup of interest makes up a small proportion of the population; the researcher divides the population into relevant subgroups and draws a sample from each to ensure representation. Cluster sampling is used when a complete list of population elements is impractical; the researcher first samples groups (clusters) of elements and then selects elements from within those groups.

Nonprobability samples are used in a variety of research contexts. To draw a convenience sample, a researcher simply collects data from those people or other relevant elements to which he or she has most convenient access. While convenience samples offer the major benefit of convenience, researchers should be cautious about generalizing from research that relies on convenience samples.

canonical_name: Survey Research: What Is It and When Should It Be Used?
candidate_draft: Survey research is a quantitative method in which a researcher poses a set of predetermined questions to an entire group or a sample of individuals. It is especially useful when a researcher aims to describe or explain features of a very large group or groups, and it is often used to explain trends or features of large populations. The method can also serve as a way of quickly gaining general details about a population of interest to help prepare for a more focused, in-depth study using time-intensive methods such as in-depth interviews or field research; in that role, a survey may help identify specific individuals or locations from which to collect additional data. Survey research is better suited to answering some kinds of research questions than others, and the way a concept is operationalized in a survey may differ from how it is operationalized in a field research study of the same topic. Survey design takes a great deal of thoughtful planning and often many rounds of revision. The method is versatile and is used across many professions: lawyers may use surveys to select juries, social service and other organizations use them to evaluate the effectiveness of their efforts, businesses use them to learn how to market their products, governments use them to understand community opinions and needs, and politicians and media outlets use them to understand their constituencies. Survey research is also a cost-effective way to gather information from many people, and because it allows data collection from very large samples at relatively low cost, it lends itself to probability sampling techniques and is well suited to gaining a representative picture of the attitudes and characteristics of a large group. Survey research tends to be a reliable method of inquiry because it is standardized: the same questions, phrased in exactly the same way, are posed to participants. However, a poorly phrased question can cause respondents to interpret its meaning differently, which can reduce that question's reliability. Survey research is a quantitative technique that complements qualitative approaches; for example, without survey research, it may not be possible to know how Americans' perspectives on race and the presidency shifted over the decades between the 1970s and the 2000s.

canonical_name: Pros and Cons of Survey Research
candidate_draft:
Survey research is a quantitative method in which a researcher poses a set of predetermined questions to an entire group or sample of individuals. It is especially useful when a researcher aims to describe or explain features of a very large group, or when a researcher needs to quickly gain general details about a population of interest to prepare for a more focused, in-depth study using time-intensive methods such as in-depth interviews or field research. In this preparatory role, a survey may help a researcher identify specific individuals or locations from which to collect additional data. As is true of all methods of data collection, survey research is better suited to answering some kinds of research question more than others; for example, a concept like political activism is likely operationalized differently in a survey than in a field research study of the same topic.

Survey research, as with all methods of data collection, comes with both strengths and weaknesses. The strengths of survey research include its cost effectiveness, generalizability, reliability, and versatility. Surveys are an excellent way to gather lots of information from many people. In one study of older people’s experiences in the workplace, a researcher was able to mail a written questionnaire to around 500 people who lived throughout the state of Maine at a cost of just over $1,000. This cost included printing copies of the seven-page survey, printing a cover letter, addressing and stuffing envelopes, mailing the survey, and buying return postage. By contrast, visiting each of those people individually to interview them in person would have required costs for gas, meals, lodging, and time, potentially doubling, tripling, or quadrupling the costs. Thus surveys are relatively cost effective.

Related to the benefit of cost effectiveness is a survey’s potential for generalizability. Because surveys allow researchers to collect data from very large samples for a relatively low cost, survey methods lend themselves to probability sampling techniques. Of all the data-collection methods described in the text, survey research is probably the best method to use when one hopes to gain a representative picture of the attitudes and characteristics of a large group.

Survey research also tends to be a reliable method of inquiry. This is because surveys are standardized in that the same questions, phrased in exactly the same way, are posed to participants. Qualitative approaches do not offer the same consistency that a quantitative survey offers. However, this is not to say that all surveys are always reliable. A poorly phrased question can cause respondents to interpret its meaning differently, which can reduce that question’s reliability.

The versatility of survey research is also an asset. Surveys are used by all kinds of people in all kinds of professions. The versatility offered by survey research means that understanding how to construct and administer surveys is a useful skill to have for all kinds of jobs. Lawyers might use surveys in their efforts to select juries, social service and other organizations (e.g., churches, clubs, fundraising groups, activist groups) use them to evaluate the effectiveness of their efforts, businesses use them to learn how to market their products, governments use them to understand community opinions and needs, and politicians and media outlets use surveys to understand their constituencies.

As with all methods of data collection, survey research also comes with a few drawbacks. First, while one might argue that surveys are flexible in the sense that we can ask any number of questions on any number of topics in them, the fact that the survey researcher is generally stuck with a single instrument for collecting data (the questionnaire), surveys are in many ways rather inflexible. If a researcher mails a survey out to 1,000 people and then discovers, as responses start coming in, that the phrasing on a particular question seems to be confusing a number of respondents, it is too late for a do-over or to change the question for the respondents who haven’t yet returned their surveys. When conducting in-depth interviews, on the other hand, a researcher can provide respondents further explanation if they’re confused by a question and can tweak their questions as they learn more about how respondents seem to understand them.

Validity can also be a problem with surveys. It can be difficult to ask anything other than very general questions that a broad range of people will understand. Because of this, survey results may not be as valid as results obtained using methods of data collection that allow a researcher to more comprehensively examine whatever topic is being studied. For example, if a researcher wants to learn something about voters’ willingness to elect an African American president, General Social Survey respondents were asked, “If your party nominated an African American for president, would you vote for him if he were qualified for the job?” Respondents were then asked to respond either yes or no to the question. But what if someone’s opinion was more complex than could be answered with a simple yes or no? What if, for example, a person was willing to vote for an African American woman but not an African American man?

Weaknesses of Survey Method As with all methods of data collection, survey research also comes with a few drawbacks. First, while one might argue that surveys are flexible in the sense that we can ask any number of questions on any number of topics in them, the fact that the survey researcher is generally stuck with a single instrument for collecting data (the questionnaire), surveys are in many ways rather inflexible. Let’s say you mail a survey out to 1,000 people and then discover, as responses start coming in, that your phrasing on a particular question seems to be confusing a number of respondents. At this stage, it’s too late for a do-over or to change the question for the respondents who haven’t yet returned their surveys. When conducting in-depth interviews, on the other hand, a researcher can provide respondents further explanation if they’re confused by a question and can tweak their questions as they learn more about how respondents seem to understand them. Validity can also be a problem with surveys. thus it can be difficult to ask anything other than very general questions that a broad range of people will understand. Because of this, survey results may not be as valid as results obtained using methods of data collection that allow a researcher to more comprehensively examine whatever topic is being studied. Let’s say, for example, that you want to learn something about voters’ willingness to elect an African American president, as in our opening example in this chapter. General Social Survey respondents were asked, “If your party nominated an African American for president, would you vote for him if he were qualified for the job?” Respondents were then asked to respond either yes or no to the question. But what if someone’s opinion was more complex than could be answered with a simple yes or no? What if, for example, a person was willing to vote for an African American woman but not an African American man?

candidate_draft: Surveys are categorized by two primary dimensions: time (when or with what frequency they are administered) and administration (how they are delivered to respondents). In terms of time, there are two main types: cross-sectional and longitudinal. Cross-sectional surveys are administered at a single point in time, providing a snapshot of respondents' attitudes or behaviors at that specific moment. A limitation of cross-sectional surveys is that they capture a static moment, making it difficult to determine if the observed phenomena remain stable over time. Longitudinal surveys, in contrast, enable researchers to make observations over an extended period, allowing them to capture changes in behavior or phenomena caused by world events or aging. There are several types of longitudinal surveys, including trend, panel, and cohort surveys, as well as retrospective surveys. Trend surveys focus on how people's inclinations change over time; the same individuals do not necessarily participate in each administration, provided the sample is representative of the population. Panel surveys involve the same group of people being surveyed repeatedly over time. Cohort surveys involve identifying a specific category of people and regularly surveying those who fall into that category. Retrospective surveys are administered only once, like cross-sectional surveys, but ask participants to report on past events, allowing researchers to gather longitudinal-like data without the time and expense of a true longitudinal study. The primary drawback of retrospective surveys is the potential for faulty recollections of past events. In terms of administration, surveys can be self-administered or conducted as interviews. Self-administered questionnaires are given to participants in writing to respond to on their own; these can be delivered in person, via mail, or online. Interviews involve a researcher posing questions directly to respondents, collecting data through personal interaction. The choice of administration method involves trade-offs: online surveys may be faster and cheaper but require respondents to have necessary hardware and internet access, while mailed surveys may reach a broader sample but are more likely to be lost or not returned.

This variety comes both in terms of time -when or with what frequency a survey is administered-and in terms of administration -how a survey is delivered to respondents. In this section we'll take a look at what types of surveys exist when it comes to both time and administration.

In terms of time, there are two main types of surveys: These surveys offer researchers a sort of snapshot in time and give us an idea about how things are for our respondents at the particular point in time that the survey is administered. I administered the survey at just one time.

Longitudinal surveys are those that enable a researcher to make observations over some extended period of time. There are several types of longitudinal surveys, including trend, panel, and cohort surveys. We'll discuss all three types here, along with another type of survey called retrospective.

The first type of longitudinal survey is called a trend survey. The main focus of a trend survey is, perhaps not surprisingly, trends. Researchers conducting trend surveys are interested in how people's inclinations change over time. The Gallup opinion polls are an excellent example of trend surveys. You can read more about Gallup on their website: http://www.gallup.com/Home.aspx. To learn about how public opinion changes over time, Gallup administers the same questions to people at different points in time. For example, for several years Gallup has polled Americans to find out what they think about gas prices (something many of us happen to have opinions about). One thing we've learned from Gallup's polling is that price increases in gasoline caused financial hardship for 67% of respondents in 2011, up from 40% in the year 2000. Gallup's findings about trends in opinions about gas prices have also taught us that whereas just 34% of people in early 2000 thought the current rise in gas prices was permanent, 54% of people in 2011 believed the rise to be permanent. Thus through Gallup's use of trend survey methodology, we've learned that Americans seem to feel generally less optimistic about the price of gas these days than they did 10 or so years ago. Because the interest here is in trends, not specific people, as long as the researcher's sample is representative of whatever population he or she wishes to describe trends for, it isn't important that the same people participate each time.

All three types of longitudinal surveys share the strength that they permit a researcher to make observations over time. This means that if whatever behavior or other phenomenon the researcher is interested in changes, either because of some world event or because people age, the researcher will be able to capture those changes. In sum, when or with what frequency a survey is administered will determine whether your survey is crosssectional or longitudinal. While longitudinal surveys are certainly preferable in terms of their ability to track changes over time, the time and cost required to administer a longitudinal survey can be prohibitive. As you may have guessed, the issues of time described here are not necessarily unique to survey research. But we’ve placed our discussion of these terms here because they are most commonly used by survey researchers to describe the type of survey administered. Finally, retrospective surveys are similar to other longitudinal studies in that they deal with changes over time, but like a cross-sectional study, they are administered only once. In a retrospective survey, participants are asked to report events from the past. By having respondents report past behaviors, beliefs, or experiences, researchers are able to gather longitudinal-like data without actually incurring the time or expense of a longitudinal survey. Of course, this benefit must be weighed against the possibility that people’s recollections of their pasts may be faulty. Imagine, for example, that you’re asked in a survey to respond to questions about where, how, and with whom you spent last Valentine’s Day. As last Valentine’s Day can’t have been more than 12 months ago, chances are good that you might be able to respond accurately to any survey questions about it. But now let’s say the research wants to know how last Valentine’s Day compares to previous Valentine’s Days, so he asks you to report on where, how, and with whom you spent the preceding six Valentine’s Days. How likely is it that you will remember? Will your responses be as accurate as they might have been had you been asked the question each year over the past 6 years rather than asked to report on all years today? candidate_draft: Designing effective questions and questionnaires is the process of creating survey items that yield usable data and presenting them in a format that respondents can easily complete. The process begins with identifying exactly what information is needed, which involves brainstorming, consulting the literature, and ranking questions to ensure the most important factors are included despite time or space limitations. When writing individual questions, researchers must avoid wording that causes confusion, such as double negatives, culturally specific terms, or double-barreled questions that ask multiple things at once. Survey questions must also be relevant to all respondents, using filter questions when necessary. When creating response options, designers must balance the problem of fence-sitting (where respondents choose a neutral option) against the problem of floating (where respondents are unsure how to categorize their answer), as solving one issue may cause the other. Pretesting is a critical step to improve the survey before administration. The final stage involves designing the questionnaire itself, which is the document containing all questions. This requires grouping questions thematically and determining the order of presentation. While there is disagreement about where to place demographic questions, the order should generally be determined by the unique characteristics of the research and the needs of the respondents to maximize completion rates and credibility.

Perhaps you wish to identify which students were comparatively more or less successful in this transition and which factors contributed to students’ success or lack thereof. Designing Questionnaires In addition to constructing quality questions and posing clear response options, you’ll also need to think about how to present your written questions and response options to survey respondents. Questions are presented on a questionnaire, the document (either hard copy or online) that contains all your survey questions that respondents read and mark their responses on. Designing questionnaires takes some thought, and in this section we’ll discuss the sorts of things you should think about as you prepare to present your well-constructed survey questions on a questionnaire. One of the first things to do once you’ve come up with a set of survey questions you feel confident about is to group those questions thematically. In our example of the transition to college, perhaps we’d have a few questions asking about study habits, others focused on friendships, and still others on exercise and eating habits. Or perhaps it would make more sense to present any questions we had about precollege life and habits and then present a series of questions about life after beginning college. Once you have grouped similar questions together, you’ll need to think about the order in which to present those question groups. Most survey researchers agree that it is best to begin a survey with questions that will want to make respondents continue (Babbie, 2010; There’s some disagreement over where on a survey to place demographic questions such as those about a person’s age, gender, and race. On the one hand, placing them at the beginning of the questionnaire may lead respondents to think the survey is boring, unimportant, and not something they want to bother completing. On the other hand, if your survey deals with some very sensitive or difficult topic, such as child sexual abuse or other criminal activity, you don’t want to scare respondents away or shock them by beginning with your most intrusive questions. In truth, the order in which you present questions on a survey is best determined by the unique characteristics of your research—only you, the researcher, hopefully in consultation with people who are willing to provide you with feedback, can determine how best to order your questions. Keeping in mind the characteristics and needs of the people you will ask to complete your survey should help guide you as you determine the most appropriate order in which to present your questions.

candidate_draft: Analysis of survey data is the process of condensing large amounts of information from completed questionnaires into usable and understandable chunks. The primary goal of this analysis is to identify, describe, and explain patterns in the data. The process typically begins with data entry, where response options are coded numerically and entered into a data analysis computer program. Researchers then run various statistical commands to identify patterns across responses. Several computer programs are designed to assist survey researchers with this task, including SPSS (Statistical Package for the Social Sciences), MicroCase, and Excel. SPSS is noted for its ability to perform both basic descriptive and complex inferential statistical analysis, while Excel is described as less sophisticated but relatively easy to use. The most basic form of analysis is univariate analysis, in which researchers describe patterns across just one variable using frequency distributions and measures of central tendency. When researchers are interested in simultaneously analyzing relationships among more than two variables, they conduct multivariate analysis. Survey data are well suited to a deductive approach, allowing researchers to analyze data to test hypotheses generated based on theories. While survey researchers should aim for the highest response rate possible, some recent research suggests that high return rates may be less important than previously thought.

The researcher may begin with an idea about likely responses to his or her open-ended questions and assign a numerical value to each likely response. Then the researcher will review participants’ open-ended responses and assign the numerical value that most closely matches the value of his or her expected response. Strengths and Weaknesses of Quantitative Interviews Quantitative interviews offer several benefits. The strengths and weakness of quantitative interviews tend to be couched in comparison to those of administering hard copy questionnaires. Quantitative interviews can also help reduce respondent confusion. If a respondent is unsure about the meaning of a question or answer option on a questionnaire, he or she probably won’t have the opportunity to get clarification from the researcher. An interview, on the other hand, gives the researcher an opportunity to clarify or explain any items that may be confusing. As with every method of data collection we’ve discussed, there are also drawbacks to conducting quantitative interviews. Perhaps the largest, and of most concern to quantitative researchers, is interviewer effect. While questions on hard copy questionnaires may create an impression based on the way they are presented, having a person administer questions introduces a slew of additional variables that might influence a respondent. As I’ve said, consistency is key with quantitative data collection—and human beings are not necessarily known for their consistency. Thus quantitative researchers may opt for written questionnaires over interviews on the grounds that they will be able to reach a large sample at a much lower cost than were they to interact personally with each and every respondent.

candidate_draft: A cross-sectional survey is a research instrument administered only once to capture a snapshot of life, events, opinions, behaviors, or other phenomena as they exist at the specific moment of administration. This single-time-point design distinguishes it from longitudinal surveys, which enable researchers to make observations over an extended period of time to track changes. The primary limitation of the cross-sectional approach is that the phenomena it assesses do not generally remain stagnant; while the survey can describe the state of the world at the moment of data collection, it is difficult to determine whether those conditions remained the same for long after the survey was administered. For example, a survey asking for opinions on terrorism on September 10, 2001, would capture a specific moment in time, but it would not reveal how those opinions evolved in the days or weeks that followed. The decision to use a cross-sectional survey is often driven by the prohibitive time and cost required to administer longitudinal surveys, making the single administration a practical alternative for gathering data. Although longitudinal surveys are generally preferable for their ability to track changes over time, the cross-sectional design remains a standard method in survey research for assessing the current state of a population.

candidate_draft: A longitudinal survey is a research design that enables a researcher to make observations over an extended period of time. This approach is used to capture changes in behavior or other phenomena, whether those changes result from world events or from people aging. The primary types of longitudinal surveys include trend, panel, and cohort surveys. A trend survey focuses on how people's inclinations change over time; for example, Gallup opinion polls administer the same questions to people at different points in time to track shifts in public opinion, such as changing attitudes toward gas prices. In trend surveys, it is not necessary for the same people to participate each time, provided the sample is representative of the population. A cohort survey involves identifying a specific category of people and regularly surveying those who fall into that category. While longitudinal surveys are preferable for tracking changes over time, they are distinguished from cross-sectional surveys by the frequency and timing of administration. The main limitation of longitudinal surveys is that the time and cost required to administer them can be prohibitive. Retrospective surveys are related but distinct; they deal with changes over time but are administered only once, asking participants to report past events. This offers the benefit of longitudinal-like data without the expense, though it carries the drawback of potentially faulty recollections.

The first type of longitudinal survey is called a trend survey. The main focus of a trend survey is, perhaps not surprisingly, trends. Researchers conducting trend surveys are interested in how people’s inclinations change over time. The Gallup opinion polls are an excellent example of trend surveys. You can read more about Gallup on their website: http://www.gallup.com/Home.aspx. To learn about how public opinion changes over time, Gallup administers the same questions to people at different points in time. For example, for several years Gallup has polled Americans to find out what they think about gas prices (something many of us happen to have opinions about). One thing we’ve learned from Gallup’s polling is that price increases in gasoline caused financial hardship for 67% of respondents in 2011, up from 40% in the year 2000. Gallup’s findings about trends in opinions about gas prices have also taught us that whereas just 34% of people in early 2000 thought the current rise in gas prices was permanent, 54% of people in 2011 believed the rise to be permanent. Thus through Gallup’s use of trend survey methodology, we’ve learned that Americans seem to feel generally less optimistic about the price of gas these days than they did 10 or so years ago. Because the interest here is in trends, not specific people, as long as the researcher’s sample is representative of whatever population he or she wishes to describe trends for, it isn’t important that the same people participate each time.

candidate_draft: A retrospective survey is a research design in which participants are asked to report events, behaviors, beliefs, or experiences from the past. It is classified as a type of longitudinal survey because it deals with changes over time, but it is distinct from other longitudinal designs because it is administered only once, similar to a cross-sectional study. The primary purpose of a retrospective survey is to allow researchers to gather longitudinal-like data without incurring the time or expense associated with administering a survey over an extended period. However, this approach involves a trade-off: the benefit of efficiency must be weighed against the possibility that participants' recollections of their pasts may be faulty. The accuracy of these reports can vary depending on how far back in time the events occurred; for instance, recalling a recent event may be more accurate than recalling events from several years prior. Retrospective surveys thus offer some of the benefits of longitudinal research but come with specific drawbacks related to memory reliability.

candidate_draft: Response rate is a metric used in survey research to measure the proportion of questionnaires that are returned in a completed and readable format. For example, if 75 out of 100 distributed questionnaires are returned completed, the response rate is 75%. While researchers do not always agree on what constitutes a good response rate, a rate of three-quarters (75%) is generally considered good or excellent by most survey researchers. candidate_draft: Fence-sitting and floating are two distinct issues in survey design related to how response options are structured. Fence-sitting occurs when respondents choose neutral response options, such as "no opinion," even if they actually have an opinion. This behavior can occur when respondents are given rank-ordered response options that include a neutral middle choice, such as a five-point scale ranging from strongly agree to strongly disagree. Floating is described as the flip side of fence-sitting. The decision of whether to allow fence-sitting or to force respondents to choose an opinion depends on the goals of the research. In some cases, allowing fence-sitting is necessary, while in others, it may be acceptable to force respondents to choose an opinion. There is a trade-off in creating response options: the solution to the problem of fence-sitting might cause floating, whereas the solution to the problem of floating might cause fence-sitting. These concepts are part of the broader process of creating effective survey questions and response options.

candidate_draft: Univariate, bivariate, and multivariate analysis are three levels of quantitative data analysis used to identify, describe, and explain patterns in survey data. Univariate analysis is the most basic form, in which researchers describe patterns across just one variable; it includes frequency distributions and measures of central tendency. Bivariate analysis assesses covariation among two variables, allowing researchers to determine whether changes in one variable occur together with changes in another. If two variables do not covary, they are said to have independence. A common procedure for bivariate analysis is to cross-tabulate the two variables and present their relationship in a contingency table. Multivariate analysis involves simultaneously analyzing relationships among more than two variables. For example, if a researcher hypothesizes that financial security declines for women as they age but increases for men as they age, adding age to an analysis of gender and financial security would require multivariate rather than bivariate analysis. The goal of these analyses is to condense large amounts of information into usable and understandable chunks, turning completed questionnaires into shareable findings.

candidate_draft: Interview research is a methodological approach used to gather detailed information and examine processes. It is particularly effective when the research topic is complex, when questions require lengthy explanation, or when participants need time and dialogue to work through their responses. A key advantage of interviews over surveys is the ability to ask follow-up questions in real time, allowing researchers to explore the story behind initial responses. This method is especially useful when researchers need to understand unique, individual narratives that cannot be captured by closed-ended survey questions. For example, interviews are well-suited for studying complex decision-making processes, such as how individuals decide not to have children and how others respond to that decision, where back-and-forth dialogue is necessary to uncover the full context.

candidate_draft: Qualitative interviews, also known as intensive or in-depth interviews, are semistructured interactions where the researcher guides a conversation to gather detailed information about a specific topic. The primary aim is to hear from respondents about what they consider important regarding the topic, captured in their own words. These interviews utilize open-ended questions, which do not provide answer options and require participants to formulate their own responses. This approach contrasts with quantitative interviewing, which relies on rigid schedules and uniform probing to minimize interviewer effects. Qualitative interviewing techniques are designed to go with the flow, allowing the interview to take the direction the respondent chooses. To support this flexibility, researchers typically develop an interview guide in advance, which serves as a non-rigid list of topics or questions to cover. A key technique in qualitative interviewing is active listening, where the researcher participates by showing understanding and following the respondent's narrative. This often involves probing, defined as a request for more information, to encourage respondents to explain or describe their experiences further. Researchers are advised to prepare helpful probes in advance and practice interviews with individuals similar to the sample to avoid being stumped during the interaction. Considerations for qualitative interviewing include acknowledging the power differential between the researcher and the participant, selecting an appropriate location, and recognizing the interview as a form of relationship. Interviewers must always be respectful of participants, a principle emphasized by feminist researchers who have helped balance power dynamics. While qualitative interviews allow for deep understanding of social processes, they have drawbacks, including reliance on the accuracy of respondents and the intensity of the process in terms of time, expense, and potential emotional strain. It is common for qualitative interviewers to take audio recordings of the interviews they conduct.

candidate_draft: Quantitative interviews are a data collection method in which a researcher poses questions directly to respondents, typically using closed-ended questions delivered in the same format and order to every participant. This approach distinguishes quantitative interviewing from qualitative interviewing, which is semistructured, uses open-ended questions, and allows the conversation to follow the respondent's lead. In quantitative interviews, probing is uniform and often predetermined; interviewers are instructed to avoid probes that might appear to agree or disagree with the respondent, using neutral acknowledgments only when explicitly requested by the participant. The primary aim of quantitative interviewing is to represent and condense data into numbers, allowing for statistical analysis. Data analysis typically involves coding response options numerically, entering these values into a data analysis program, and running statistical commands to identify patterns. Quantitative interviews offer advantages over self-administered questionnaires, such as the ability to clarify confusing items and potentially higher response rates. However, they carry the drawback of interviewer effect, where the presence of a human administrator introduces variables that may influence responses, and they are generally more time-consuming and expensive than written surveys. All interviewers, including those using quantitative techniques, must consider the power differential between themselves and respondents, choose appropriate interview locations, and maintain respect for participants.

If possible, it is also best to include nonverbals in an interview’s written transcription. Gestures made by respondents should be noted, as should the tone of voice and notes about when, where, and how spoken words may have been emphasized by respondents. I never cease to be amazed by the things I recall from an interview when I transcribe it myself. If the researcher who conducted the interview transcribes it himself or herself, that person will also be able to make a note of nonverbal behaviors and interactions that may be relevant to analysis but that could not be picked up by audio recording. An interview guide is a list of topics or questions that a researcher develops in advance to guide the interviewer during a qualitative interview. It is not a rigid script; rather, it functions like an agenda or to-do list, allowing the interviewer to cover key areas while adapting to the participant's responses. In qualitative interviewing, the guide outlines issues the researcher considers important, but the flow of the interview is shaped by the participant's own words and priorities. The specific format of an interview guide can vary based on the interviewer's style and experience, ranging from a brief outline of topic headings to a detailed list of specific questions. Researchers may create two versions of a guide: a detailed version for preparation and practice, and a brief outline to use during the actual interview to encourage active listening and avoid the impression that the interviewer is more interested in their questions than the participant's answers.

The construction of an interview guide is a deliberate process that typically begins with brainstorming all relevant topics and questions. The researcher then refines this list by removing redundancies, grouping similar items, and creating thematic headings. It is also recommended to consult scholarly literature to identify questions used in similar studies. When ordering the guide, sensitive or controversial questions should generally be avoided at the beginning to allow participants to warm up. The guide should primarily use open-ended questions to allow participants to share information in their own words. Follow-up questions should be used to probe for more detail, but phrasing should be non-confrontational; for example, asking "Could you tell me a little more about that?" is preferred over asking "why," which can feel hostile. A focus group is a qualitative data collection method defined as a planned discussion designed to elicit group interaction and obtain perceptions on a defined area of interest in a permissive, nonthreatening environment. Unlike one-on-one qualitative interviews, where the researcher primarily acts as a listener and question asker, focus groups are more dynamic and rely on the group interaction as a key focal point. The researcher takes the role of a moderator, posing questions or topics for discussion and then allowing group members to discuss the question or topic among themselves. Participants may ask each other follow-up questions, agree or disagree with one another, display body language that reveals their feelings about the conversation, or even come up with questions not previously conceived of by the researcher. These interactions and displays are of direct interest to the researcher, who aims to get participants talking to each other and to observe interactions among participants.

Group size should be determined in part by the topic of the interview and the likelihood that participants will have much to say without much prompting. If the topic is one about which participants feel passionately and will have much to say, a group of 3–5 is ideal. Some recommend that a group of about 6–10 participants is the ideal size for focus group research. In terms of focus group composition, homogeneity of background among participants is recommended while diverse attitudes within the group are ideal.

Focus groups share many of the strengths and weaknesses of one-on-one qualitative interviews. Both methods can yield very detailed, in-depth information and provide researchers with an opportunity to observe participants' body language. Focus groups offer the added benefit of giving researchers a chance to collect data on human interaction by observing how group participants respond and react to one another. Focus groups can be expensive and time-consuming, though there may be some time savings as it takes fewer group events than one-on-one interviews to gather data from the same number of people. A potential drawback of focus groups, which is not a concern for one-on-one interviews, is that one or two participants might dominate the group, silencing other participants. Careful planning and skillful moderation on the part of the researcher are crucial for avoiding, or at least dealing with, such possibilities. Focus groups are used in a variety of professions, from market research to academia to government and political research, and are a useful method for researchers who wish to gather in-depth information about social processes.

Field research is a qualitative method of data collection aimed at understanding, observing, and interacting with people in their natural settings. In this context, being in 'the field' means being out in the real world and involved in the everyday lives of the people being studied. Field research functions as an umbrella term that encompasses the myriad activities field researchers engage in when collecting data, typically involving a combination of participant observation, interviewing, and the analysis of documents or artifacts created by the people observed. The method has its origins in anthropology, and researchers sometimes use the terms ethnography or participant observation to refer to this specific approach.

Field research is used when researchers seek to gain firsthand experience and knowledge about the people, events, and processes they study. It provides a close-up lens on everyday life, allowing for the collection of very detailed data about people and processes, often more detailed than what can be obtained using other methods. It is an excellent method for understanding the role of social context in shaping people’s lives and experiences, enabling a greater understanding of the intricacies and complexities of daily life. A unique strength of field research is its ability to uncover elements of people’s experiences or group interactions of which researchers were not previously aware. Unlike interviews and surveys, where respondents cannot provide information they are not aware of, field research typically occurs over an extended period of time, allowing social facts that may not be immediately revealed to be discovered over the course of the project.

Field notes are the first and necessary step toward developing quality analysis in field research, serving as the record that affirms what a researcher observed. They are not to be taken lightly or overlooked as unimportant. Writing field notes is a skill that can be improved with practice; conducting field research and taking field notes are decidedly not informal activities, and observation in field research is deliberate, not haphazard. Understanding when to write, what to write, where to write, and how to write are all skills that field researchers develop with experience.

There are two different kinds of field notes: descriptive and analytic. Descriptive field notes are notes that simply describe a field researcher’s observations as straightforwardly as possible; they typically do not contain explanations of or comments about those observations, and the observations are presented on their own, as clearly as possible. Analytic field notes are notes that include the researcher’s impressions about their observations. Though the lines between what counts as “description” and what counts as “analysis” can get pretty fuzzy, the distinction is nevertheless useful when thinking about how to write and how to interpret field notes.

Writing and analyzing field notes involves moving from description to analysis. Analyzing field note data is a process that occurs over time, beginning at the moment a field researcher enters the field and continuing as interactions are happening in the field, as the researcher writes up descriptive notes, and as the researcher considers what those interactions and descriptive notes mean. Often field notes will develop from a more descriptive state to an analytic state when the field researcher exits a given observation period, messy jotted notes or recordings in hand, and sits at a computer to type up those notes into a more readable format. Field researchers typically spend several hours typing up field notes after each observation has occurred. This is often where the analysis of field research data begins. Having time outside of the field to reflect upon thoughts about what has been seen and the meaning of those observations is crucial to developing analysis in field research studies. Once the analytic field notes have been written or typed up, the field researcher can begin to look for patterns across the notes by coding the data.

The strategy for recording observations while in the field is determined mostly by the site chosen and the role played in that site. Writing notes while in the field requires a fine balance between jotting down observations and actually engaging in the setting. If a researcher is strictly an observer, these are easy to balance; but if also a participant, note taking should not keep the researcher from participating. In locations where taking notes “in the moment” would be too obvious, rude, or distracting, a researcher may still occasionally jot down a few things very quickly, or develop a way of jotting down observations that doesn’t require complete sentences or perhaps even words. Some field researchers have developed their own version of shorthand to take notes, using some combination of abbreviations and symbols, without taking too much time away from their participation in the field. Field researchers use a variety of strategies to take notes while in the field, including jotting notes on their hands and arms, keeping very small notebooks in their pockets, carrying small recorders to make quick observations, and even writing notes on toilet paper during visits to the restroom. With the advent of smartphones, taking notes in the field has become less arduous than it once was.

This is one type of writing where the aim is not to go for literary value, to make the writing interesting, or even to make it readable for anyone other than the researcher.
